title: Inhibition of circulating glycocholic acid-regulated signaling potentiates immune checkpoint therapy in colorectal cancer

paper_content.abstract:
Serum bile acids (BAs) emerge as risk factors for cancer, but their roles in colorectal cancer (CRC) remain unclear.
We show that glycocholic acid (GCA), a primary BA, is elevated in the serum of CRC patients. In a mouse CRC
model, GCA promotes tumor programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression in tumors, suppressing CD8⁺ T cell-
mediated antitumor immunity and facilitating tumor growth. Mechanistically, GCA inhibits the BA receptor farnesoid
X receptor (FXR), a transcriptional repressor for SRY-box transcription factor 14 (SOX14). Loss of FXR repression
upregulates SOX14-mediated expression of zinc finger DHHC-type palmitoyl transferase 9 (DHHC9), thereby
reducing PD-L1 palmitoylation and stabilization. Silencing SOX14 or DHHC9, or activating FXR, synergizes with
anti-PD-1 therapy, reducing tumor growth in GCA-treated mice. These findings uncover a mechanism that GCA
remodels the tumor microenvironment to mediate CRC resistance to immunotherapy, highlighting therapeutic
opportunities targeting the FXR-PD-L1 axis in CRC patients with elevated serum GCA.
paper_content.introduction:
Colorectal cancer (CRC) represents one of the main causes of mortality.1, 2 Previous studies have shown that
programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)-expressing tumor cells attenuate CD8+ T cell infiltration, which results in tumor
progression.3 Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies, including anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-
1)/PD-L1 or anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 therapies, have changed the therapeutic landscape and
provided an unprecedented clinical response in various types of cancer.3, 4, 5 Although ICB therapy has durable effects
toward a subset of microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) CRCs, accounting for ~15% of all CRC cases, only 30-50%
of these patients can benefit from this therapy.6 Regrettably, patients with microsatellite instability stable
(MSS)/proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) (~85%) merely have a 5-10% response rate. Metabolic reprogramming
contributes to tumor immune evasion and progression, which is also considered as an important hallmark in tumors.
It has been shown that metabolic reprogramming in CRC regulated by cholesterol or fatty acids is sufficient to reshape
the tumor microenvironment (TME), leading to resistance towards ICB therapy.7, 8, 9, 10 Therefore, the identification of
key metabolites in regulating resistance to PD-L1 therapy is necessary to combat an immunosuppressive TME in CRC.

The expression of PD-L1 in tumor cells is regulated by various processes, including transcription and post-
transcriptional modifications (PTMs).11 During cell malignant transformation and tumor initiation, the transcription
level of PD-L1 is associated with oncogenic pathways such as aberrant activation of WNT/β-catenin and RAS/MAPK
signaling.12, 13 Moreover, PATMs, including palmitoylation, are critical for regulating the protein stability and function
of PD-L1, and consequentially leading to reduced anti-tumor immunity in the TME. 14 It has been demonstrated that
metabolic stress alters palmitoyl transferase-induced protein palmitoylation.14, 15 Notably, the palmitoyl transferases
zinc finger DHHC-type palmitoyl transferase (DHHC)3 and DHHC9 have been reported as key regulators for
mediating the palmitoylation of PD-L1, which contributes to lysosome sorting during PD-L1 degradation in several
types of cancer.14, 16 Thus, to identify whether and how metabolic alterations in CRC regulate the effects of PD-L1
palmitoylation is important for improving ICB therapy.

Bile acids (BAs) are considered as important regulators of intestinal epithelial homeostasis in the gastrointestinal tract.
In addition to their detergent properties,17 BAs serve as ligands to nuclear (hormone) receptors such as the farnesoid
X receptor (FXR), thus controlling numerous important cellular metabolism, regulatory and signaling functions, as
well as immune responses.18 In CRC, circulating levels of BAs are strongly associated with tumor initiation and
progression.19, 20 However, activation of FXR negatively regulates intestinal cancer stem cell proliferation, leading to
a slower CRC progression.21 Therefore, the role of BAs in regulating tumor initiation and development is still
controversial, and it remains unknown whether alterations in BAs-mediated signaling in tumor cells may affect
immune surveillance and ICB sensitivity.

The present study demonstrated that FXR inactivation mediated by the serum primary BA glycocholic acid (GCA) in
CRC is necessary and sufficient to inhibit the antitumor response of CD8+ T cells. Mechanistically, GCA increased
the expression of the transcription factor (TF) SRY-box transcription factor 14 (SOX14) by inhibiting FXR
transcription-suppressing function, and consequentially promoted the DHHC9-induced palmitoylation and
stabilization of PD-L1. Notably, activation of FXR with the agonist GW4064 sensitized ICB-resistant CRC to anti-
PD-1/PD-L1 treatment. Taken together, the present findings indicate that targeting the FXR signaling pathway is a
potential strategy for alleviating immunosuppressive TME and enhancing the sensitivity to anti-PDL-1 treatment in
CRC.
paper_content.results:
Increased serum GCA in patients with CRC is associated with poor clinical prognosis. It has been suggested that
the elevation of serum BAs is associated with higher risk for multiple cancer types22, however, the association between
BAs and CRC remains to be elucidated. To investigate whether BAs and which BA is associated with CRC
tumorigenesis, we collected serum samples from 80 patients with CRC (Cohort1) and 20 healthy individuals, and
measured the levels of 33 kinds of BAs including primary free, secondary free, primary conjugated and secondary
conjugated BAs by ultra performance LC-MS. It was found that only 6 BAs, that is, glycocholic acid (GCA),
taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TDCA), taurocholic acid (TCA), taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA),
glycochenodeoxycholic acid (GCDCA) and glycodeoxycholic acid (GDCAS) were differently expressed, what’s more,
all of these 6 BAs were significantly upregulated in the sera of patients with CRC compared with healthy individuals.
Notably, the concentration of GCA was mostly upregulated compared with the other five types of BAs in patients
with CRC (Fig. 1A). It was also found that the levels of GCA in patients with CRC with stage III/IV or distal metastasis
were higher than those found in patients with CRC with stage I/II or without metastasis (Fig. 1B and C). In addition,
increased levels of GCA were positively associated with poor 5-year disease-free and overall survival (Fig. 1D and
E). Univariate and multivariate survival analyses further indicated that serum GCA served as an independent
prognostic biomarker for poor outcome in patients with CRC (Fig. S1A and B). Furthermore, we validated our results
by using an additional CRAC cohort, and confirmed that the serum concentration of GCA was increased in patients
with stage III/IV or distal metastasis (Fig. S1C and D), leading to worse disease-free and overall survival (Fig. S1E
and F). In addition, higher serum GCA concentrations remained significantly associated with both shorter disease-
free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) in CRC patients without liver metastasis (Fig. S1G and H). Take together,
these results indicated that upregulated serum GCA in CRC patients was associated with poor prognosis.

GCA promotes tumor growth in a mouse model of CRC via inhibiting FXR activity. As BAs mainly function by
regulating FXR signaling in the intestine,17, 19 we then examined the effects of FXR with its agonist GW4064 on the
CRC cell lines MC38, CT26, HCT116 and SW620. As expected, activation of FXR by GW4064 significantly
promoted FXR activity (Fig. 1F and S2A). FXR was knocked out in MC38, CT26, HCT116 and SW620 cells with
the CRISPR/Cas9 system (Fig. S2B), and it was found that GW4064 failed to promote FXR activity in Fxr-deficient
mouse and human CRC cells (Fig. S2C). Next, we cultured MC38 cells with 0-200µM of GCA and observed that
GCA suppressed FXR activity in a dose dependent manner (Fig. S2D). Of note, 100nM of GCA robustly decreased
the activation of FXR without affecting the proliferation of MC38 cells, suggesting that this dosage of GCA is optimal
for in vitro experiments (Fig. S2D). Consistently, same tendency was observed in other CRC cells (Fig. 1F and S2A).
And GCA inhibited the transcriptional expression of the FXR downstream genes SHIP and IBABP in these CRC cell
lines confirmed by qPCR (Fig. 1G and S2E). Given that BAs regulate FXR function by altering the expression of FXR
or the ability binding to RXR, which is required for its downstream transcriptional activity23, we performed qPCR as
well as immunoprecipitation experiments, and found that GCA inhibited the interaction between FXR and RXR,
without affecting the mRNA level of FXR itself (Fig. S2F and G). In addition, we also observed that the FXR agonist
was sufficient to restore the expression of SHIP and IBABP in GCA treated MC38 and HCT116 cells (Fig. S2H),
suggesting a negative role of GCA in FXR signaling in CRC.

To further explore the roles of GCA in CRC, MC38, CT26, HCT116 and SW620 cells were incubated with GCA or
GW4064, and it was observed that the treatment had little effect on tumor cell proliferation in vitro (Fig. S2I).
Consistently, the proliferation rate was also comparable in both FXR-deleted (FXR-KO) and control CRC cells (Fig.
S2J). However, by using intestinal epithelial-specific Fxr-knockout (Fxr-ko, Fxr-/-) mice, it was found that Fxr was
successfully deleted in intestine tissues and AOM/DSS-induced tumors (Fig. S2K-L). Loss of FXR promoted the
development of CRC, as evidence by a decreased the colorectal length in the Fxr-ko mice, (Fig. 1H). Histological
analysis showed that tumors derived from Fxr-ko mice exhibited enlarged size and poor differentiation (Fig. 1I). We
also generated another orthotopic mice model of CRC by implanting Fxr-knockout and control MC38 cells into colon
mucosa. Consistently, mice with Fxr-knockout tumors showed an increased tumor growth and a worse overall survival
compared to that of control tumors (Fig. S3A), suggesting that FXR acted as a tumor suppressor in CRC tumorigenesis
in vivo. To further confirm this result, we inoculated MC38 cells into C57BL/6 mice and observed that 400 mg/kg of
GCA treatment (intragastric gavage; ig) robustly increased tumor burden without evident side effects as measured by
weight loss during the cause (Fig. S3B). We next measured the concentrations of BAs significantly elevated in the
serum of CRC patients in mice following GCA administration (400 mg/kg). While serum and tumoral GCA levels
were barely detectable in tumor-bearing mice without GCA treatment, GCA-treated mice exhibited measurable
accumulation, with serum levels reaching approximately 150 nM and tumoral concentrations around 82 nmol/g (Fig.
S3C-D). Notably, the median serum GCA concentrations in human Cohorts I and II were approximately 96.4 nM and
96.7 nM, respectively. These values are comparable to, or slightly lower than, those observed in GCA-treated mice,
supporting the physiological relevance of our experimental model.

Of note, GCA significantly increased the tumor growth in AOM/DSS-induced CRC models, as evidenced by an
increased tumor numbers and a short colon length in mice treated with GCA (Fig. S3E). However, GCA-treatment
could not further promote the tumorigenesis in Fxr-ko C57BL/6 mice, suggesting that FXR is the functional target of
GCA-induced tumorigenesis. While GCA significantly promoted tumor growth and decreased overall survival in
immunocompetent mice by subcutaneously inoculating MC38 or CT26 cells (Fig. S3F and G), no significant
difference was observed in terms of tumor size or survival rate between the GCA-treated and control groups when
MC38 or CT26 cells were inoculated in immunodeficient BALB/c nude mice (Fig. S3H and I). qRT-PCR showed that
GCA suppressed FXR signaling pathway in vivo, as shown by decreased expression of SHIP and IBABP in MC38 or
CT26 tumors derived from immune-competent or nude mice treated with GCA (Fig. S3J and K). To avoid the potential
effects of bacterial transformation of GCA in intestine, we intraperitoneal injected (i.p.ed) GCA twice a week in MC38
tumor-bearing mice and found an increased tumor growth in mice with GCA treatment (Fig. S3L). Collectively, our
data indicated that immune responses played an important role in the GCA-induced development of CRC.

Based on the ability of GCA to inhibit FXR-activity, the present study next investigated whether altering the function
of FXR could affect GCA-mediated tumor growth. Indeed, increased tumor size and decreased survival rate were
observed in immunocompetent mice, but not in BALB/c nude mice, when treating the animals with the FXR antagonist
T-βMCA (Fig. 1J and S4A-B), which mimics the behavior of tumor inoculated in immunocompetent mice or in
immunodeficient mice treated with GCA. Consistently, the suppressive role of FXR in cancer was confirmed when
immunocompetent, but not immunodeficient, BALB/c nude mice were treated with the FXR agonist GW4064 (Fig.
S4C-G). To explore whether impaired FXR signaling was critical for GCA-increased tumor growth in vivo, the mice
were treated with GCA in the absence or presence of the FXR-agonist GW4064 after inoculating MC38 or CT26 cells.
As expected, mice receiving GW4064 showed decreased tumor size and prolonged overall survival compared with
mice treated with GCA alone (Fig. 1K and S4H). Of note, GW4064 reverted the expression of FXR target genes I-
BABP and SHP that inhibited by GCA (S4I and J). Taken together, these data suggested that impairment of FXR-
mediated tumor suppression was critical for GCA-induced tumorigenesis, and immune responses were involved in
regulating the GCA-FXR axis mediated tumor development.

GCA treatment inhibits CD8+ T cell infiltration and antitumor response. To further investigate the effects of
tumor-infiltrated immune cells on GCA/FXR-mediated tumor progression, five independent cell clusters of CD45+
immune cells, including B cells, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, macrophages and natural killer cells, were identified based
on scRNA-seq (Fig. 2A right). An increased total number of CD8+ T cells and macrophages was observed in tumors
treated with GW4064 compared with those without treatment (Fig. 2A left). The expression of markers of immune
subtypes was shown by using a panel of 21 markers (Fig. S5A). Next, MC38 tumors were isolated from mice receiving
GCA (i.g.) for 10 days, and the percentages of subpopulations in immune cells were analyzed by flow cytometry.
Consistently, CD8+ T cells and macrophages, but not CD4+ T cells or CD4+ Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Treg), were
downregulated in tumors treated with GCA (Fig. 2B). To explore whether the suppressive effect of FXR on tumors
was dependent on CD8+ T cells or macrophages, CD8+ T cells or macrophages were depleted in mice by using an their
specific anti-CD8α antibody or clodronate liposomes (Fig. S5B), respectively, before inoculating the mice with MC38
cells with or without GCA or GW4064 treatment. Notably, GCA treatment did not further increase tumor growth in
CD8+ T cell-depleted mice compared with untreated controls (Fig. 2C). Moreover, it was also found that the FXR
agonist failed to inhibit CRC tumor progression in CD8+ T cell-depleted mice (Fig. 2D). However, tumor growth was
comparable in both macrophage-depleted and control mice regardless of GCA or GW4064 treatment (Fig. 2E and F).
In addition, MC38 or CT26 CRC cells were inoculated into Rag1-/- mice (which are deficient in T and B cells), and it
was observed that treatment with FXR antagonist or agonist had a limited effect on tumor growth in Rag1-/- mice (Fig.
S5 C and D). These data suggested that CD8+ T cells, but not macrophages, in the TME were involved in GCA/FXR-
mediated tumor growth.

We next explore the signaling pathway enriched in GCA-induced tumorigenesis, single-cell RNA sequencing analysis
revealed that genes upregulated in FXR signaling-mediated activated tumors were mainly associated with immune
responses, including type I/II IFN responses (Fig. S6A and B). We examined the expression of IFN-stimulated genes
(ISGs), including CXCL9, CXCL10, BST2, STAT1 and IFITM3, by qPCR. As expected, the mRNA levels of these
ISGs were significantly upregulated in MC38 and CT26 tumor tissues derived from immunocompetent mice treated
with GW4064 (Fig. S6C), whereas the expression of ISGs were decreased in tumors treated with GCA (Fig. S6D).
However, the alteration of the mRNA levels of ISGs was not observed in tumor tissues derived from immunodeficient
BALB/c nude mice when treating with GW4064 or GCA (Fig. S6E and F). Interestingly, MC38 and HCT116 cells
were also treated with GW4064 or GCA in culture, however, no significant increase in the transcriptional expression
of these ISGs was observed in GW4064- or GCA-treated CRC cells (Fig. S6G and H), suggesting a dependency on
IFN signaling associated immune responses in vivo.

As IFNγ is critical for tumor suppression mediated by CD8+ tumor-infiltrated T cells, we further used FACS analysis
to evaluate IFNγ-expressing CD8+ T cells. It was found that IFNγ-expressing CD8+ T cells were significantly
decreased in GCA-treated MC38 or CT26 tumors (Fig. 2G, S6I). However, an increased frequency of exhausted PD-
1+ TIM3+ CD8+ T cells was observed in tumors treated with GCA compared with controls (Fig. 2G and S6I). On the
contrary, tumors treated with FXR agonist GW4064 showed an enhanced population of CD8+ IFNγ+ T cells,
accompanied with attenuated exhausted CD8+ T cell infiltration (Fig. 2H and S6J). Thus, the present results suggested
that GCA-induced FXR impaired the antitumor activity of CD8+ T cells in the TME.

Increased expression of PD-L1 is required for GCA-mediated tumorigenesis. To investigate the underlying
molecular mechanisms of GCA-mediated suppression of T cell immune responses, data-independent acquisition MS-
based proteomics was performed in MC38 cells treated with or without GCA. Heatmap showed that PD-L1 was the
most significantly increased protein among the top 20 deferentially expressed proteins (FC≥2, p≤0.05) annotated to
both cytokine production and regulation of immune response pathways in GCA-treated MC38 cells (Fig.2I). Next,
CRC cells were treated with GCA or GW4064 in vitro, and the changes in the mRNA and protein levels of PD-L1
were evaluated. It was found that the levels of protein and cell surface expression of PD-L1, but not its mRNA levels,
were upregulated in tumor cells treated with GCA (Fig. 2J and S7A, C). By contrast, PD-L1 protein levels were
decreased in MC38 cells treated with the FXR agonist GW4064 compared with untreated cells (Fig. 2J, S7B and C),
which suggests that the GCA/FXR-mediated increase in PD-L1 was regulated in a post-transcriptional manner.
Functionally, tumor infiltrated CD8+ T cells were co-cultured with MC38 cells or CT26 cells that had been pre-
pretreated with GCA under anti-CD3 and anti-CD28-stimulating conditions, and it was found that FXR-inactivation
rendered CRC cells more resistant to CD8+ T cells in T cell-mediated tumor cell-killing assays (Fig. S7D). Furthermore,
tumor cell killing capacity was increased in wild-type (WT), but not in Cd274-KO, CRC cells pre-treated with a FXR
agonist (Fig. S7E). We further corroborated the results with in vivo subcutaneous tumor growth model and found that
knockout of Cd274 in MC38 cells or CT26 cells significantly reverted GCA-induced tumorigenesis (Fig. 2K and L).
qRT-PCR analysis revealed that CD274-knockout did not affect GCA-induced suppression of FXR downstream genes
I-BAPA and SHP (Fig. S7F and G). While low-dose anti-PD-L1 (10mg/kg) therapy have minimal effect on tumor
suppression in GCA-treated mice with subcutaneous tumors or in Fxr-/- mice of AOM/DSS-induced CRC model,
blockade of PD-L1/PD-1-signaling with a high-dose of anti-PD-L1 (100 mg/kg) effectively reversed GCA-induced
tumorigenesis (Fig. S7H-J), suggesting that increased PD-L1 expression in tumors is critical for GCA/FXR-mediated
dysfunction of CD8+ T cells during tumor growth.

GCA accelerates PD-L1 palmitoylation via DHHC9 in tumor cells. Since GCA treatment did not alter the
transcriptional levels of PD-L1 in CRC cells, we next suppressed the common degradation pathways that are involved
in the regulation of PD-L1. It was observed that GCA-mediated total and surface PD-L1 accumulation was reversed
by 2-bromopalmitate, a general palmitoylation inhibitor, not by the autophagy inhibitor 3-MA or the proteasome
inhibitor MG-132 in CRC cells (Fig. 3A and B). Similarly, increased expression of PD-L1 was observed in CRC cells
treated with palmostatin B, the inhibitor of acyl protein thioesterase 1, which promotes global palmitoylation, in a
dose-dependent manner (Fig. 3C). Moreover, GCA enhanced the palmitoylation modification of PD-L1 in CRC cells
according to the results of Click-iT labelling assay, indicating that GCA stabilized the PD-L1 protein via
palmitoylation (Fig. 3D).

To explore the key palmitoyltransferases for GCA-mediated PD-L1 accumulation, the transcriptional levels of
palmitoyltransferases were screened by RNA-sequencing analysis, and it was found that the expression levels of
DHHC9, DHHC1, DHHC1A2, DHHC18 and DHHC24 were on the top rank of differentially expressed genes in GCA-
treated cells compared with controls (Fig. 3E). Then we knocked down these candidates in MC38 and HCT116 CRC
cells by using specific siRNAs and found that GCA-induced accumulation of the total and cell surface PD-L1 protein
was significantly reduced in DHHC9-knockdown CRC cells but not in other palmitoyltransferases-knockdown CRC
cells (Fig. 3F and G). In addition, the transcriptional levels of DHHC9 were significantly upregulated in GCA-treated
CRC cells confirmed by qPCR (Fig. S8A). To further investigate the function of DHHC9 in regulating the
palmitoylation modification on PD-L1, DHHC9 was overexpressed in CRC cells. Increased protein, but not mRNA,
expression of PD-L1 was observed in DHHC9-ovexpressing CRC cells (Fig. 3H and S8B). Notably, the palmitoylation
modification on PD-L1 was significantly accumulated with the overexpression of DHHC9 (Fig. 3I). Next, we
evaluated whether DHHC9 was critical for GCA-mediated PD-L1 expression. As expected, a decreased protein
expression, but not transcriptional expression, of PD-L1 was observed in DHHC9-knockdown cells treated with GCA
(Fig. S8C and D). Functionally, it was found that the tumor cell killing capacity of tumor-derived CD8+ T cells was
significantly increased when co-cultured with DHHC9-knockdown CRC cells even without treatment with GCA (Fig.
3J). By contrast, overexpressing DHHC9 in MC38 or CT26 cells decreased the killing capacity of CD8+ T cells,
leading to increased tumor growth (Fig. 3K). Furthermore, this tumor promoting capacity could not be reversed by
treatment with the FXR agonist GW4064 (Fig. 3K). Collectively, these results indicated that DHHC9-mediated
palmitoylation modification was critical for the GCA/FXR-induced stabilization of PD-L1 and tumor growth.

The SOX14-DHHC9 axis regulates PD-L1 expression in CRC cells. To identify the TF(s) which is (are) responsible
for the GCA-mediated regulation of tumor PD-L1 expression, we analyzed all the differentially expressed
transcriptional factors with fold change (FC) ≥ 2 in CRC cells treated with GCA, and it was observed that SOX14 was
on the top list of the candidate TFs in terms of FC in expression (Fig. 4A). Loss-of-function screenings were then
performed using specific siRNAs target to top 5 candidate TFs. The results showed that knockdown of SOX14, but
not other candidates, could significantly diminish the expression of PD-L1 protein in CRC cells (Fig. 4B). Moreover,
the mRNA expression of FXR downstream gene IBABP was negatively associated with SOX14 expression in tumor
tissues derived from 80 patients with CRC (Fig. 4C upper). Subsequently, we explored whether FXR directly inhibited
SOX14 transcription. The promoter region of human SOX14 was screened for FXR-binding site by using the JASPAR
database, and ChIP assay was performed with an anti-FXR antibody under GCA or GW4064 treatment conditions. It
was observed that FXR directly bound to the promoter of SOX14 (site 2), as evidenced by the enrichment of the target
sequence (Fig. S9A). Moreover, GCA inhibited the DNA-binding capacity of FXR, whereas the FXR agonist GW4064
promoted its binding with DNA in CRC cells. (Fig. S9B). Finally, luciferase reporter constructs were generated to test
the transcriptional activity of WT and FXR-binding sequence deficiency mutated regions for FXR-binding sites (site
2). As expected, the luciferase activity was significantly increased in HCT116 and SW620 cells transfected with WT
region constructs upon GCA stimulation (Fig. S9C). By contrast, GW4064 significantly decreased the luciferase
activity of CRC cells with WT region constructs, but not of cells transfected with mut region constructs (Fig. S6C),
suggesting that FXR acts as a transcriptional suppressor for SOX14 expression. It was also found that knockdown of
SOX14 decreased PD-L1 expression by using shRNA targeting SOX14 in multiple CRC cell lines even though treated
with GCA (Fig. 4D left, E, and S9D-F). Of note, increased protein levels of PD-L1 were observed in SOX14-
overexpressing cells (Fig. 4F left and G, and S9E), suggesting that increased SOX14 expression may be involved in
GCA-induced PD-L1 expression. Moreover, we also investigated whether SOX14 was involved in regulating GCA-
mediated tumor promoting function by inoculating SOX14-knockdown cells into the subcutaneous tissue or colon
mucosa of mice treated with GCA. Then, we found that Sox14 deficiency inhibited GCA-induced tumor growth,
which was accompanied by an increased frequency of tumor-infiltrating total CD8+ T cells, as well as CD8+ IFNγ+ T
cell subset, but a decreased number of exhausted CD8+ T cells in both subcutaneous and orthotopic CRC model (Fig.
4H and I, S9G and H). The data indicated that SOX14 was a key TF in regulating GCA-mediated PD-L1 expression.

To identify whether SOX14 directly regulates DHHC9 expression, we firstly analyzed the correlation between the
mRNA expression of SOX14 and DHHC9 in 80 human CRC samples, and found that SOX14 was positively correlated
with DHHC9 mRNA expression (Fig. 4C down). It was also validated that GCA significantly increased the
transcription and protein expression of SOX14 and DHHC9, as well as PD-L1 protein expression, in murine MC38
and human HCT116 cells (Fig. 4D right and E). However, knockdown of SOX14 decreased the transcriptional
expression of DHHC9, as well as the protein levels of both DHHC9 and PD-L1 in CRC cells when treated with GCA
(Fig. 4D right and E). By contrast, increased DHHC9 and PD-L1 expressions were observed in CRC cells with SOX14
overexpression compared with control cells (Fig. 4F right and G). Most importantly, FXR-mediated DHHC9 and PD-
L1 inhibition could be reversed by overexpression of SOX14 in cells incubated with a FXR agonist (Fig. 4F right and
G), suggesting that SOX14 is a potent FXR downstream TF for inducing DHHC9 transcriptional expression. Next,
we analyzed the JASPAR database and identified two SOX14-binding sequences on the promoter region of human
DHHC9 by ChIP assay. Only the predicted site 1binding sequence was enriched in ChIP-enriched promoters (Fig. 4J
and K). Moreover, luciferase reporter constructs with SOX14-binding deficiency mutated regions for SOX14-binding
were generated to evaluate transcriptional activity, and found that luciferase activity was significantly increased in
SOX14-overexpressing MC38 and HCT116 cells transfected with DHHC9 WT region constructs, but not in cells
transfected with DHHC9mut region constructs (Fig. 4L). This indicated that SOX14 was critical for DHHC9
expression.

Next, we examined whether DHHC9 was involved in SOX14-mediated tumor progression by overexpressing DHHC9
in SOX14-knockdown CRC cells. We found that overexpression of DHHC9 increased the expression of PD-L1 in
CRC cells that exhibited downregulated PD-L1 expression by SOX14-knockdown (Fig. S9I). And overexpression of
DHHC9 blocked SOX14 deficiency-mediated tumor inhibition (Fig. S9I). In addition, overexpression of DHHC9 in
SOX14-deficient cells led to increased infiltration of total CD8+ T and CD8+ IFNγ+ T effector cells, but decreased
infiltration of exhausted PD-1+ TIM3+ CD8+ T cells (Fig. S9J). Taken together, these data revealed that DHHC9 was
the transcriptional and functional target of SOX14.

The GCA-mediated SOX14/DHHC9 axis correlates with decreased efficacy of immunotherapy in CRC patients.
To further understand the role of the GCA-regulated SOX14/DHHC9 axis in immunotherapy in patients with CRC,
LC-MS analysis was performed in the serum of 41 patients with MSI-H mCRC who received PD-1 blockade alone or
combination with chemotherapy. The majority of patients with mCRC (15/20) with high levels of GCA were predicted
non-responsive for immunotherapy, while patients with mCRC (19/21) with low concentrations of GCA showed
response to immunotherapy (Table S2). Magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography showed that patient
27 had a relatively high level of serum GCA and tumor progression after PD-1 blockade treatment (Fig. 5A, left and
C), whereas patient 14, with a low concentration of serum GCA, showed tumor regression (Fig. 5A, right and C).
We also examined SOX14 and DHHC9 proteins by using IF in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissues from
patients with mCRC who received PD-1 blockade. The majority of mCRC patients with high concentrations of serum
GCA showed strong SOX14, DHHC9 and PD-L1 staining accompanied by low number of CD8+ T cells and often
insensitivity to anti-PD-1 therapy (Fig. 5B and C). On the contrary, patients with low levels of serum GCA exhibited
opposite results (Fig. 5B and C). Furthermore, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis revealed a significant correlation
between the high levels of GCA, SOX14, DHHC9 and PD-L1 and shorter progression-free survival (PFS) rates of
patients with mCRC who received anti-PD-1 therapy (Fig. 5D-G). Conversely, higher number of infiltrated intratumor
CD8+ T cells were accompanied by prolonged PFS rates in patients with CRC who received anti PD-1 therapy (Fig.
5H). Spearman correlation analysis showed that SOX14 protein expression was positively correlated with DHHC9
and PD-L1 protein expression in CRC tumor samples according to the IF staining scores (Fig. 5I and J). DHHC9
protein expression was also positively associated with PD-L1 protein (Fig.5K). We further confirmed our results that
the serum level of GCA was associated with the expression of DHHC9 or SOX14 in tumors of CRC patients in another
cohort (Fig.S10 A-B). Additionally, DHHC9 staining was correlated with SOX14 staining in these CRC tumors
(Fig.S10C). Altogether, these results suggested that GCA regulated SOX14/DHHC9/PD-L1 axis played significant
role on the efficacy of immunotherapy in mCRC, which may be useful as potential prognostic markers for PD-1
blockade in future.

Inhibition of GCA/FXR-induced SOX14 and DHHC9 expression sensitizes CRC to anti-PD-1 therapy. To
explore whether the SOX14-DHHC9-PD-L1 axis is critical for GCA/FXR-mediated immunosuppression, it was
hypothesized that Sox14-knockdown (Sox-KD) could ameliorate anti-PD-1 treatment in CRC under high levels of
GCA in the TME. Then, GCA-treated immunocompetent mice were engrafted with control or Sox14-KD CRC cells
and found that knockdown of Sox14 inhibited MC38 colon cancer outgrowth in the presence of anti-PD-1 therapy
(Fig. 6A). Moreover, increased infiltration of CD8+ T and CD8+ IFNγ+ T effector cells, while decreased exhausted
CD8+ T cells were observed in Sox14-KD cells compared with control cells in mice with and without anti-PD-1
antibody (Fig. 6B). Consistently, knockdown of Dhhc9 also significantly suppressed tumor growth in mice subjected
to anti-PD-1 therapy compared with mice with monotreatment. In addition, Dhhc9-deficiency enhanced the CD8+ T
cell anti-tumor function in the TME, as evidenced by the proportion of CD8+ T and IFNγ+ CD8+ T enriched in Dhhc9-
knockdown MC38 tumors with anti-PD-1 treatment (Fig. 6C and D). As GCA negatively regulated FXR activity, we
further investigated whether a FXR agonist could synergize CRC cells to anti-PD-1 therapy. As expected, combined
GW4064 and anti-PD-1 treatment robustly slowed the tumor growth, which as associated with a higher number of
CD8+ IFNγ+ T effector cell infiltration and lower percentage of exhausted T cells in tumors compared with those
receiving monotherapies, suggesting that the activation of FXR sufficiently promoted the antitumor effects of anti-
PD-1 therapy (Fig. S11A-D). In addition, anti-PD-1 therapy slightly decreased the AOM/DSS-mediated CRC
tumorigenesis in both C57ABL/6 and BALB/c mice (Fig. S11E-F). Of note, we observed that mice treated with
combined anti-PD-1 and GW4064 were most likely to benefit from therapy, as evidenced by an increased colon length
with a decreased tumor numbers and areas in mice receiving combined treatment compared to mono-treatment (Fig.
S11E and F). To strengthen the present conclusions, anti-PD-1-resistant MC38 (MC38R) colon cancer was generated
by three rounds of in vivo/in vitro selection. Anti-PD-1 antibody had a limited effect on the growth of MC38R cells
in both subcutaneous and orthotopic CRC models (Fig. 6E and F, S11G and H). However, GW4064 inhibited MC38R
tumor growth and sensitized MC38R cells to anti-PD-1 therapy, which was accompanied by a significantly increased
antitumor response of CD8+ T cells, as evidenced by increased infiltration of CD8+ T and CD8+ IFNγ+ T effector cells,
and decreased exhausted CD8+ T cells in tumors compared with GW4064 monotreatment (Fig. 6E and F, S11G and
H). The data indicated that combining FXR agonist with anti-PD-1 therapy enhanced the efficacy of anti-PD-1 in
resistant colon cancer.
paper_content.methods:
Patient biopsies. A total of 80 paired CRC tissues, adjacent normal mucosa tissues and serum collected between
January 2018 and September 2018 from patients with CRC who were diagnosed at Fudan University Shanghai Cancer
Center (FUSCC) were used for measuring the concentrations of a series of BAs and for tissue immunofluorescence
staining (cohort Ⅰ). In addition, the serum of 20 normal healthy individuals was collected in October 2018. Furthermore,
41 patients with MSI-H or dMMR with recurrence or distant metastasis who received anti PD-1 immunotherapy
between February 2019 and September 2021 at FUSCC were enrolled in the present study (cohort Ⅱ). A cohort of 308
patients (Cohort III) with colorectal cancer (CRC) was enrolled between January 2008 and September 2009 at Fudan
University Shanghai Cancer Center. Their clinicopathological characteristics of the patients are summarized in
Supplementary Data 1-3. All patients from these 3 cohorts did not receive any treatment for cancer before surgery.
Human serum specimens were collected prior to tumor resection, while normal mucosa and paired cancer tissues, as
well as metastatic tissues, were collected immediately after surgical resection. Written informed consent was obtained
from each patient, and the study protocol both conformed to the ethical guidelines of the 1975 Declaration of Helsinki
and was approved by the Ethics Committee of FUSCC (approval no. 050432-4-2108).

Cell lines, plasmids, lentivirus production and transduction. The HCT116 and SW620 human colon cancer cell
lines, the CT26 mouse colon cancer cell line, and the 293T cell line were obtained from the American Type Culture
Collection, while the MC38 mouse colon cancer cell line was purchased from the Cell Bank of the Institute of
Biochemistry and Cell Biology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Cell lines were cultured at 37˚C in 5% CO2 in
DMEM or in RPMI1640 supplemented with 10% fetal calf serum, 100 U/ml penicillin and 100 µg/ml streptomycin.
Cells were tested monthly and found to be free of mycoplasm by PCR-based screening. Full-length SOX14 and
DHHC9 fused with Flag-tag were amplified via PCR from cDNA of HCT116 cells, and then recombined into the
pLVX plasmid (cat. no. 125839; Addgene, Inc.). The primers used are listed in Supplementary Data 4. Short hairpin
RNA (shRNA) sequences targeting SOX14 and DHHC9 were cloned into the pLKO.1 vector (cat. no. 10878; Addgene,
Inc.), and the primers used are listed in Supplementary Data 5. Single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting FXR or CD274
were constructed into the lentiCRISPR v2 vector (cat. no. 52961; Addgene, Inc.). CRISPR/Cas9 targeting sequences
are listed in Supplementary Data 5. Lentivirus was produced by transiently transfecting 293T cells with
Lipofectamine® 3000 transfection reagent (cat. no. L3000075; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) according to the
manufacturer’s instructions. The viral supernatants were then incubated with 8 μg/ml Polybrene for 24 h, and the viral
supernatants were then exchanged for fresh media. Cells were incubated for 48 h before puromycin selection. For
small interfering RNA (siRNA) transfection, tumor cells were seeded into 6-well plates at ~1.5x105 cells per well and
incubated at 37˚C overnight. Specific siRNAs (5 nM; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) were transfected into cells and
incubated for 6 h. Next, the medium was replaced with complete DMEM for 48 h. The siRNA sequences are listed in
Supplementary Data 6. The anti-PD1-resistant MC38R tumor cells were developed as previously described.37 In brief,
6-week-old C57BL/6J mice were injected subcutaneously into the right flank with 1.0x106 MC38 cells (n=6). At 10
days post-injection, mice were treated twice weekly with 100 μg anti-PD-1α antibody (Bio X Cell) per mouse via
intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection for 1 week. Next, tumors were selected and transplanted into the right flank of 6-week-
old C57BL/6J mice. After 3 repeated cycles of tumor selection, nonresponsive tumors were digested into single tumor
cells, namely MC38R tumor cells.

Sample preparation and HPLC-MS/MS-based metabolomic approaches.
100 μl serum were spiked with 0.51 ml of ice-cold MeOH-ACN (1:1, v:v). The sample was vortexed and incubated
for 1h at - 20 °C, following by centrifuging at 14000 rcf at 4 °C for 15 min to precipitate proteins. The supernatant
was aspirated, evaporated using a vacuum concentrator (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The extracts were
reconstituted in 100 μl of MeOH and deionized water (85:15, v:v), and centrifuged at at 15000 g at 4 °C for 15 min to
remove insoluble debris. The supernatant was collected at UPLC autosampler vials (Thermo Scientific, MA, USA)
and stored at - 80 °C prior to UPLC-MS analysis. Tumor samples were homogenized in 100% acetonitrile and were
centrifuged twice at 15,000g for 30 minutes at 4°C for removal of precipitated proteins and other particulates to remove
precipitated proteins and particulates. The supernatant was then diluted with 0.1% formic acid. The quality control
sample was pooled by mixing 5 μL of extracted solution from each sample.

Liquid chromatographic separation and mass spectrometric detection were conducted using the Thermo Scientific
TSQ Quantum Ultra LC-MS/MS system (Thermo Fisher, Palo Alto, CA). Chromatographic separation was achieved
on a Poroshell SB-C18 analytical column (particle size, 1.7 μm; 50 mm (length) × 2.1 mm (i.d.)) equipped with a BEH
C18 VanGuard pre-column (5 × 2.1 mm, i.d.; 1.7 μm). The mobile phase consisted of aqueous buffer containing 1 mM
ammonium formate and formic acid (pH 4.39) (A) and acetonitrile/isopropanol (1:1 v/v) (B), with a total flow rate of
0.4 ml/min. The gradient profile for the LC pumps was as follows: 20–30% B (0-3 min), 30-40% B (3-4 min), 50-70%
B (4-5 min), 70-90% B (5-5.2 min), continuing at 90% B up to 6 min. The injection volume for all samples was 2 μl.
The column temperature was set to 55 °C, and the sample tray temperature was maintained at 8 °C. For mass
spectrometric detection, the electrospray ionization (ESI) source was operated in negative ion mode to produce
MS/MS spectra (Thermo Fisher). The parameters were as follows: spray voltage 2 kV, cone voltage 30 V, source
temperature 120 °C, desolvation temperature 500 °C, cone gas flow 50 L/h, desolations gas flow 900 L/h.

For preparation of standard stock, 33 bile acid were dissolved to 1 mg/mL by appropriate amount of methanol as
standard stock solutions and then further diluted to obtain standard solutions containing 0.05, 0.5, 5, and 50 mg/mL
of each bile acid. The supernatant was collected and 70 μl was injected into the LC–MS/MS system for analysis.
Cholic acid (CA), chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA), sodium glycochenodeoxycholate (GCDCA), sodium
taurochenodeoxycholate (TCDCA), glycocholic acid (GCA), taurolithocholic acid (TLCA), sodium
taurodeoxycholate hydrate (TDCA), and taurocholic acid sodium salt hydrate (TCA) was purchased from Sigma-
Aldrich (Saint Louis, MO). Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), deoxycholic acid (DCA). Lithocholic acid (LCA) and
glycoursodeoxycholic acid (GUDCA) were procured from Cayman Chemical Company (Ann Arbor, MI, USA).
Glycodeoxycholic acid (GDCA) and glycolithocholic acid (GLCA) were acquired from Toronto Research Chemicals
(TRC, Canada).

Data‐independent acquisition mass spectrometry (MS)‐based proteomics. MC38 cells were treated with or
without GCA for 24 h and processed by Data Independent Acquisition6 individually to assess the proteome. In brief,
for sample preparation, cells were lysed in lysis buffer (1% SDS and 8 M urea) and digested with iST Sample
Preparation kit (PreOmics) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Peptides were eluted with elution buffer (2 x
100 µl) and then lyophilized by SpeedVac. Protein samples were reconstituted in 0.1% FA and subjected to UltiMate
3000 liquid chromatography (LC) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.). In total, 200 ng peptide was separated by an
analytical column with a 60 min gradient starting at 4% buffer B (80% ACN with 0.1% FA), followed by a stepwise
increase to 28% in 25 min, 44% in 10 min, 90% in 10 min, hold for 7 min, and then equilibration at 4% for 8 min. The
column flow rate was maintained at 500 nl/min with a column temperature of 50˚C. DIA data were acquired in the
diaPASEF mode. Raw data of DIA were analyzed by Spectronaut 17 (Biognosys AG) with default settings. The
normalization strategy was set to local normalization. Peptides which passed the 1% Q-value cut-off were used to
calculate the major group quantities with the MaxLFQ method. Differentially expressed proteins were selected based
on P<0.05, fold-change (FC)>1.5 or FC<1/1.5.

Dual Luciferase Reporter Assay. For measurement of FXR activity, cells were seeded into 24-well plates at ~1.5x104
cells per well and transfected with the FXR luciferase reporter plasmid FXRE-Luc (200 ng; cat. no. 11764ES03;
Shanghai Yeasen Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) and 20 ng Renilla pRL-SV40P plasmid (cat. no. 27163; Addgene, Inc.) per
well with Lipofectamine® 3000 according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Next, cells were treated with GCA
(100nM, cat. no. G2878; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck KGaA) or GW4064 (5μM, cat. no. G5172; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck
KGaA) for 24 h, and the relative luciferase units (RLUs) were measured using the Dual-Glo Luciferase Assay System
(Promega Corporation) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For monitoring SOX9 or DHHC9 expression,
cells were seeded and transfected with 200 ng pGL3-SOX14, pGL3-SOX14-FXR mutant 15, pGL3-DHHC9 or pGL3-
DHHC9-SOX14 mut vector, along with 20 ng Renilla pRL-SV40P plasmid per well with Lipofectamine® 2000. After
24 h, the RLUs in cells were measured using the Dual-Glo Luciferase Assay System. The firefly RLUs were
normalized by the RLUs from the Renilla-containing vector.

Mice. Fxr floxed mice were purchased from Cyagen Biosciences, Inc. (cat. no. S-CKO-04890). Villin-Cre (#004586)
transgenic mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME, USA) to create conditional knockout
mice and silenced the expression of Fxr in intestinal epithelial cells. Briefly, two synthesized sgRNAs targeting introns
3 and 4, Cas9 mRNA and LoxP-containing oligonucleotide flanking with 50-bp homology arms were injected into
mouse zygotes and then transferred into pseudo-pregnant mice. Fxr floxed mice were identified by genotyping and
sequencing. Fxr floxed mice were then crossed with villin-Cre transgenic mice to obtain intestinal epithelial-specific
Fxr knockout mouse models. The mice were randomly assigned into experimental groups. For primary mouse models,
animals were chosen based on correct genotypes and were co-allocated in the same cages and used for the studies. All
mice used in the study were gender- and age-matched. Investigators were blinded to the treatments during the
experiments. All mice were housed in the specific-pathogen free animal facility of FUSCC. Animals were observed
for general health and signs of distress (reduced weight, ruffled fur, or evidence of tumor ulceration/bleeding). Mice
were euthanized when body weight loss exceeded 20% or when tumor volume exceeded 1,500 mm³. Euthanasia was
performed in accordance with institutional and guidelines by CO₂ inhalation followed by cervical dislocation to ensure
death. The maximal tumor burden permitted by our ethics committee is 1,500 mm³, and this limit was not exceeded
in any experiment. All animal procedures were approved by the Animal care and Use Committee of FUSCC.
For tumor engraftment, 6-week-old C57BL/6J or BALB/c mice were injected subcutaneously into the right flank with
1.0x106 MC38 or CT26 cells, respectively. BALB/c nude mice were also used to establish a subcutaneous CRC model
by using MC38 or CT26 cells. The tumor volumes were calculated by using the formula ‘length x width x width/2’ at
the indicated days. Body weight was recorded at the time of tumor measurement. For survival analysis, mice were
considered moribund and euthanized when tumor volume reached approximately 1000 mm³ or when severe signs of
distress were observed. For endoscopy-guided orthotopic mouse model, wild-type 10-12 weeks old C57BL/6 mice
were examined by endoscopy Coloview® system (Storz, Tuttlingen, Germany) with a zero-degree optic (diameter 1.9
mm) to ensure the colonic mucosa was healthy prior to implantation after anesthesia. For tumor cell implantation, the
colon was first washed with PBS at 37 °C and 0.5×106 MC38 cells) diluted in 50 μL of PBS were injected very slowly
towards the lumen of lower mid and distal colon ~30 mm from the anal verge to induce tumor growth by using
endoscopic injection. The tumor volume was endoscopically monitored weekly by endoscopic score. For the
AOM/DSS-induced colitis-associated cancer model, 8 to 10-week-old male mice were injected i.p. with 10 mg/kg
AOM (cat. no. A5486; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck KGaA). After 5 days, 2% DSS (cat. no. D8906; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck
KGaA) was added to the drinking water for 5 days, followed by regular drinking water for 2 weeks. The mice were
sacrificed after 3 repeated cycles of DSS. For the macrophage-depletion experiment, the mice were pretreated with
clodronate liposome (150 μl; Max Scientific) 3 days before inoculating with tumor cells, and then the indicated mice
were administered with clodronate and control liposomes, with or without GCA [400 mµg/kg, intragastric gavage (ig)
or GW4064 (50 mg/kg, i.p.)] twice per week during the course of the experiments. For the CD8-depletion experiment,
mice were treated with an anti-CD8 antibody (200 µg per injection; clone 2.43; Bio X Cell) twice weekly during the
course of the experiments. For anti-PD-1 antibody treatment, mice were treated with 100 μg anti-PD-1α antibody (Bio
X Cell) per mouse twice weekly or the corresponding IgG control via i.p. injection for the indicated days. For anti-
PD-L1 antibody treatment, mice were treated with 10 mg/kg or 100mg/kg anti-PD-L1 antibody (Bio X Cell) per mouse
twice weekly or the corresponding IgG control via i.p. injection for the indicated days. For GCA (400 mg/kg,
intragastric gavage), GW4064 (50 mg/kg, i.p.) or T-βMCA (400 mg/kg, i.p.) treatment, mice were treated with
GW4064 or T-βMCA twice per week after 6 days of being inoculated with the indicated CRC cells.

mRNA extraction and reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Total RNA was extracted from cells
or tumors by using TRizol® reagent (cat. no. 15596026CN; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) according to the
manufacturer’s instructions. Next, the extracted RNA was reversely transcribed to cDNA with PrimeScript® RT
Reagent Kit (cat. no. RR037B; Takara Bio, Inc.). RT-qPCR was conducted with a fast two-step amplification program
using FastStart Universal SYBR Green Master Mix (cat. no. 04913850001; Roche Diagnostics GmbH). Data were
normalized to GAPDH. The primers used are listed in Supplementary Data 7.

Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay. HCT116- and SW620-expressing SOX14-Flag CRC cells, or CRC
cells treated with GCA or GW4064 for 24 h, were subjected to ChIP assay with SimpleChIP® Enzymatic Chromatin
IP Kit (cat. no. 9003S; Cell Signaling Technology, Inc.) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Mouse monoclonal
antibody specific for FXR (cat. no. 72105; Cell Signaling Technology, Inc.) and rabbit monoclonal antibody specific
for SOX14 (cat. no. PA1-28074; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) were used for ChIP assay. SYBR Green RT-qPCR
was performed by using the following primers: FXR binding site 1 forward: 5’-TTTGTATTTCAAGCCCTAA-3’ and
reverse: 5’-GACTTCGGTTCCACATTGT-3’; FXR binding site 2 forward: 5’-CAGTCTAGAGCTAGCCTCT-3’ and
reverse: 5’-CGCACCTGCCAACACGCCGG-3’; SOX14 binding site 1 forward: 5’-
AGGGAGATGGGTGGAGGAGT-3’ and reverse 5’-CGGCCGCCCCTATC-3’; and SOX14 binding site 2 forward:
5’-GGAGGCGCCGAGGCC-3’ and reverse: 5’-CCCACCACTGGCCAAAT-3’.

Immunoblotting. For immunoblotting, samples harvested form cells or tumors were lysed with RIPA buffer (cat. no.
89901; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) supplemented with a protease inhibitor (cat. no.
05892970001; Roche Diagnostics GmbH) and a phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (cat. no. 04906845001;
Roche Diagnostics GmbH) for 1 h. The lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4˚C. The supernatants
were collected, and equal quantities of cell lysates (100 μg) were mixed with 5X SDS-PAGE loading dye. Next, the
samples were separated using 10% SDS-PAGE and transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes (MilliporeSigma). The
membranes were then incubated with the indicated primary and secondary antibodies and visualized using the
SuperSignal West Dura Extended Duration Substrate (cat. no. 34076; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.). The antibodies
employed are listed in Supplementary Data 8.

Immunofluorescence microscopy and multiplex immunofluorescence staining. For immunofluorescence
microscopy assay, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, followed by permeabilization with 0.5%
Triton X-100 for 15 min. Samples were blocked with 1% goat serum for 30 min, and then incubated with the indicated
primary antibodies at 4˚C for 12 h before being incubated at room temperature with secondary antibodies conjugated
to Alexa Fluor 488/594. DAPI (cat. no. ab104139; Abcam) was used to stain the nuclei for 30 min before subjecting
the samples to Zeiss Axiovert-200 fluorescence microscope (Zeiss AG).

For multiplex staining, samples were treated following the Opal protocol staining method. The reagents used were as
follows: Anti-SOX14 (cat. no. #ab214041; 1:500; Abcam), anti-DHHC9, anti-PD-L1 and anti-CD8 (cat. no. 98941;
Cell Signaling Technology, Inc.; RRID: AB_2756376, 1:500) antibodies were visualized by using fluorescein-cyanine
(Cy) 7 (1:50), fluorescein-Cy5 (1:50) and fluorescein-Cy3 (1:50). In addition, DAPI (1:2,000) was used for nuclei
staining. All sections were cover slipped using VECTASHIELD Hardset Antifade Mounting Medium (cat. no. #H-
1400; Vector Laboratories). The slides were scanned, and the mean fluorescence intensity of the indicated markers
was analyzed with a Vectra slide scanner (PerkinElmer, Inc.) under fluorescence conditions.

Co-culture assay. MC38 or CT26 cells were injected (1.0x106 cells) subcutaneously into the right flank of C57BL/6
or BALB/c mice for 2 weeks. Next, the CD8+ T cells in MC38 or CT26 tumors were isolated by FACs. The number
of indicated MC38 cells or CT26 cells was counted after 3 days of co-culture with CD8+ T cells (1.0x104 cells) in the
presence of anti-CD3 (5 μg/ml) and anti-CD28 (5 μg/ml) antibody.

Tumor digestion, cell isolation and flow cytometry analysis. Tumors derived from the indicated mice were sheared
and digested by using digestion buffer [RPMI medium supplemented with 5% FBS, intravenous collagenase I (0.5
mg/mL, cat. no. C1-22; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck KGaA) and DNase (1 µg/ml; cat. no. D5025; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck
KGaA) for 30 min at 37˚C. Next, the mixture was filtered, and red blood cells (RBCs) were lysed using RBC lysis
buffer (cat. no. 00-4300-54; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.). The precipitates were washed with buffer II (PBS with
2% FBS) and blocked with anti-CD16/32 antibody for 30 min. The single-cell suspensions were washed and incubated
with the indicated antibodies before being subjected to LSRII (BPD Biosciences) for analysis. Data were analyzed using
FlowJo. The antibodies used are listed in Table S8. Cell populations were identified based on the following expression
markers: CD4 T cells: CD45+/CD4+; CD8 T cells: CD45+/ CD8+; MDSC cells: CD45+/CD11b+/Gr-1+; and
macrophages: CD45+/CD11b+/F4/80+. For intracellular staining, cells were stimulated with phorbol 12-myristate 13-
acetate (20 ng/ml; cat. no. p8139; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck KGaA), ionomycin (1 μg/ml; cat. no. 13909; Sigma‐Aldrich;
Merck KGaA) and brefeldin A (5 ng/ml; cat. no. B5936; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck KGaA) for 4 h and then stained
according to the intracellular cytokine staining procedure. Gate strategy (Fig.S12) and representative image of tumors
(Fig.S13) were shown in supplementary Figures.

Single cell sorting, library preparation and sequencing and data preprocessing. Tumor single-cell suspensions
were prepared and filtered over 40-µm cell strainers. Next, cell concentration and viability were evaluated by Trypan
Blue staining. The isolated cells were subjected to single cell RNA analysis. In brief, cells were loaded to prepare
single-cell gel beads in emulsions (GEMs) by using Chromium Single Cell Controller Instrument (10x Genomics).
GEMs were encapsulated using the Single Cell 3’ Library & Cell Bead Kit (10x Genomics). Completed libraries were
sequenced by Illumina NovaSeq 6000 using high-output 75-cycle kits with 150-bp paired-end reads. The data files
were analyzed with the R package SingleR. Gene transcript counts per cell and was determined by the unique
molecular identifier (UMI; R package Seurat, version 3.1.1). After removing low-quality cells and likely multiplet
captures, Seurat (normalizeData function) was used to normalize the expression values for each cell by the total
expression and log-transformed the results. FindVariableGenes function in Seurat was performed to identify the highly
variable genes. Then, these genes were subjected to RunPCA function and FindClusters function of Seurat to calculate
the significant principal components. The clusters were visualized in a two-dimensional t-SNE algorithm using the
RunTSNE function in Seurat and the marker genes of each cluster were identified by The FindAllMarkers function in
Seurat. Additionally, differentially expressed genes (DEGs, P< 0.05 and |log2 (fold-change)| >0.58) was filtered by
the FindMarkers function. Then, SingleR, was used for unbiased cell type recognition of scRNA-seq, with the
reference transcriptomic datasets ‘Human Primary Cell Atlas’ to infer the origin of each single cell independently and
to identify cell types.38 Gene Ontology enrichment pathway enrichment analyses of DEGs were carried out using the
hypergeometric distribution of R software. For immune cells, CD45+ cells were gated, and five major clusters of
immune cells were identified, including CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, macrophages, B cells, neutrophils and NK cells
by using markers for inferring immune cell populations in time-of-flight (CyTOF) analysis as previous study39.
Sequencing and bioinformatics analysis were performed by Shanghai OE Biotech Co., Ltd.

PD-L1 palmitoylation. Tumor cells were co-cultured with complete medium containing 100 μM Click-iT Palmitic
Acid-Azide (cat. no. C10265; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) at 37˚C and 5% CO2 for 6 h. Next, the cells were
harvested and lysed with lysis buffer (1% SDS in 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0) supplemented with a protease inhibitor
and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail on ice for 0.5 h. After sonication, the cell lysate was centrifuged at 12,000 x g at
4˚C for 10 min. The supernatants of cell lysates were collected and subject to Click-iT assay by using the Click-iT
Protein Reaction Buffer Kit (cat. no. C10276; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) following the manufacturer’s
instructions. The biotin-alkyne (cat. no. 901995; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck KGaA) connected palmitic-protein complex
was followed by streptavidin (cat. no. 3419; Cell Signaling Technology, Inc.) pull-down and immunoblot assay for
PD-L1.

Statistical analysis. Statistical analyses were performed by using GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software; Dotmatics).
No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. No data was excluded from the analyses. For data showing
normal distribution, the statistically significant differences between 2 groups of samples were estimated by applying
an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests. One-way ANOVA and Dunnett’s post hoc test were used for comparison
between ≥3 groups. The log-rank test was also applied to assess statistical significance in survival data. Statistical
significance (p-values) was defined as not significant (ns): p > 0.05; *: p < 0.05; **: p < 0.01; ***: p < 0.001. All of
the experiment was independently performed 3 times, each yielding similar results; data from one representative
independent experiment is presented as the mean ± SD.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a highly prevalent tumor type that is generally refractory to immunotherapy. Thus, elucidating mechanisms of CRC resistance to immunotherapy is of high importance. In this study, Zhao et al make use of a comprehensive range of clinical data, in vivo models, and in vitro cell biology assays to identify bile acids as potential regulators of CRC sensitivity to T cell attack. Mechanistically, this is proposed to occur through the bile acid nuclear receptor Fxr, which regulates expression of SOX14 and the palmitoyltransferase DHHC9 to control palmitoylation and stability of the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1. Overall, the experiments appear to have been generally well-executed (although the methodological details are not always clear, nor is it clear how often experiments were reproduced). The connection between bile-acid/Fxr-dependent regulation of tumor PD-L1 expression is not well understood in the context of CRC, but a similar set of observations were recently published for hepatocellular carcinoma (Gong et al, Norcholic Acid Promotes Tumor Progression and Immune Escape by Regulating Farnesoid X Receptor in Hepatocellular Carcinoma, Front Oncol, 2021).
Overall, the data are interesting and shed light on a mechanism of PD-L1 regulation that is not well understood. However, I have several concerns that should be addressed prior to publication.
Major concerns:
1. Fig. 1b/c: GCA concentrations are noted on the y-axis as ‘relative concentration’, but what are they relative to? The median differences between early and late-stage disease (panel B) or localized vs metastatic disease (panel C) may be statistically significant but are less than 0.1 in log2 space, which equates to a <7% difference. Are these difference considered biologically or clinically meaningful? Is it possible to estimate bile acid concentrations in tumor tissue?
2. Fig. 1d/e and Fig. S1a/b: elevated circulating bile acid concentrations are typically associated with hepatic dysfuncton(resulting in impaired clearance of bile acids from portal blood). This raises the question of whether the increased GCA concentrations observed in patients with metastatic CRC are due to liver metastases impairing hepatic functon(as opposed to a causative role of GCA in promoting CRC progression, as implied in this manuscript). It would be interesting/informative to compare BA concentrations in patients with liver vs non-liver metastases, and include liver metastasis specifically as a covariate in survival analysis (as distinct from other metastatic sites).
3. Fig. 1f/h/i (DSS-AOM data): the DSS-AOM model data are intriguing, but somewhat challenging to interpret. The DSS-AOM regimen models colitis-associated CRC, which follows a distinct process of pathogenesis compared to the much more common sporadic CRCs (which are the principal focus of this manuscript). Most importantly, tumorigenesis in this system relies on repeated rounds of DSS-driven colitis, and tumor burden is associated with the severity of DSS-driven tissue damage. Because the authors appear to have used mice with constitutive loss of Fxr in intestinal epithelial cells (Fxr.flox crossed with Villin-Cre), it is not possible based on these data to determine whether Fxr function is associated with alterations in tumorigenesis, colitis, or both. One potential alternative is to use mice with inducible Villin-controlled Cre (Vill.Cre.ERT2) so that Fxr can be deleted in colon epithelial cells after the final round of DSS (to exclude effects on colitis). However, the challenge of interpreting colitis-associated CRC data in the context of a paper that's focused on sporadic CRC remains. If the authors' intent is simply to generate data using an orthotopic model of CRC, alternative systems could include direct implantation of CRC cell lines into colon mucosa, or delivery of CRC cells to the liver via hydrodynamic tail vein injection.
4. Treatment with GCA apparently reduces activity of FXRE significantly in the luciferase reporter system (cell line assays). What is the source of the basal reporter signal? Is this an overexpression artifact, or are the cells exposed to bile acids in culture medium (possibly via serum)?
5. Figure 2I: The authors report that treatment of MC38 cells with GCA significantly induced PDL1 expression at the protein level, but not at the mRNA level. PDL1 is well-known to be an interferon-inducible gene, and it is noteworthy that several other proteins identified by the authors as induced by GCA are also known to be interferon-inducible, including Ifi204, B2m, Mndal, and H2-M3. Is this merely a coincidence, or is it possible that GCA-treatment is inducing an autocrine type I IFN response? Have the authors performed an unbiased transcriptional analysis (e.g. bulk RNAseq) to determine if such an interferon-like response is indeed occurring?
6. Fig. S4H/I: the apparent dependency of Fxr-driven tumor growth effects on tumor PDL1 expression is interesting and important to the overall message of the paper. To exclude the possibility that this phenotype is driven by clone-to-clone differences, can this observation be further supported by blocking PDL1 in tumors from wild type cells (e.g. with anti-PD-L1 blocking antibody) in the presence or absence of Fxr ligands?
7. Figure 5: the authors propose that the Fxr-regulated SOX14/DHH-C9/PD-L1 axis is involved in resistance of MSI-H/dMMR CRC patients to anti-PD-1 therapy in the clinic. This conclusion seems potentially odd—if we assume that tumor-expressed PD-L1 acts by engaging PD-1 on T cells, and if the anti-PD-1 antibody (the specific identity of the treatment regimen should be stated in methods) was dosed adequately to fully inhibit PD-1, then why would increased expression of PD-L1 on tumor cells have any bearing on anti-PD-1 response? Is there any reason to believe that these patients did NOT receive a dose of anti-PD-1 sufficient for full target coverage?
8. Figure 6 (and various associated statements in text): along a similar line, the authors propose that inhibition of SOX14 or DHHC9 expression in tumors causes an improved anti-tumor immune response and improved tumor control, presumably via reduced PD-L1 expression. While this makes sense under untreated conditions, they argue that this also applies during treatment with anti-PD-1. Similar to the clinical setting, unless PD-1 blockade is substantially incomplete, it is difficult to understand why alterations in tumor PD-L1 expression would enhance sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. The data instead raise the possibility that tumor-intrinsic SOX14/DHHC9 deficiency can act at least partially in a PD-L1-independent fashion to increase tumor sensitivity to immune surveillance and anti-PD1 treatment.
9. The MC38 and CT26 models used extensively in this manuscript best represent the inflamed and potentially immunotherapy-responsive MSI/dMMR subset of CRC. Have the authors explored whether manipulation of the Fxr pathway impacts immune responses to 'colder' tumor models that are more representative of sporadic MSS/pMMR CRCs (which constitute the vast majority of CRC and the bulk of unmet clinical need). For example, this could include engineered colon organoids (e.g. Taraborelli et al, Nat Comm, 2023).
Minor concerns:
1. Extensive grammatical and spelling errors throughout manuscript. English-language editing recommended.
2. Heatmap scales are generally missing units/labels throughout the figures.
3. Page 8, lines 162-165: The statement here is confusing and should be clarified. Should it actually say, “FXR-mediated tumor suppression…”?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Zhao et al. demonstrated that glycocholic acid (GCA) enhances tumor cell PD-L1 expression, thereby suppressing CD8+ T cell-mediated antitumor responses in the tumor microenvironment (TME) and promoting colorectal cancer tumor growth. This effect is mediated through the targeting of the FXR/SOX14/DHHC9 axis. The study also suggests a testable hypothesis: inhibiting GCA/FXR signaling could augment the effectiveness of anti-PD-L1 therapy. While this study presents a novel and intriguing perspective with potential implications for immunotherapy in colorectal cancer (CRC) patients, several major concerns need to be addressed, and the conclusion lacks robust evidence.
Specific comments are the following:
1. The authors mention the measurement of 34 bile acids (BAs) in serum but fail to provide a detailed description of the method and BA profiling data. Additionally, the criteria for defining low and high GCA levels in the recruited population are not clearly explained. This GCA-based subgrouping method lacks validation in another cohort.
2. The authors assert that GCA acts as an FXR antagonist based on the Luciferase reporter assay. However, intra-gastric gavage feeding in animal experiments with GCA or TβMCA treatment raises concerns about the potential impact of bacterial transformation of GCA in the gastrointestinal tract. Alternative administration methods, such as intraperitoneal injection, should be considered.
3. The logical flow of the narrative appears disrupted with the introduction of Result 2 [GCA inhibits IFN signaling in vivo].
4. The statement "Since GCA-induced PD-L1 expression was dependent on post-transcriptional modification" (Line 243) lacks a clear reference or supporting data.
5. Inconsistencies between figure arrangement and subtitles of results and figure legends are noted. For instance, Figure 1F-K implies that GCA-increased CRC tumorigenesis is FXR-dependent, but this is not accurately reflected in the subtitle of Result 1 or Figure 1. Additionally, Figure 2, described as "GCA impairs the antitumor effect of CD8 T cell by increasing tumor intrinsic PD-L1 expression," lacks validation data (Cd274-KO data should be rearranged).
6. Line 377 mentions investigating whether inhibition of GCA/FXR could sensitize CRC to anti-PD-L1 therapy, but the subjects were treated with anti-PD1 therapy. Clarification is needed.
7. Representative tumor graphs for all in vivo animal experiments should be provided by the authors.
8. Lines 467-468 discuss the discussion of an FXR agonist with the antibiotic metronidazole enhancing GCA-induced resistant tumors to ICB therapy without presenting relevant data about the antibiotics.
9. Detailed recruitment criteria information for the two cohorts, including healthy subjects, should be provided.
10. The abstract mentions a "GCA diet" (Line 27), but there is no related information about it in the animal method, which relies on intragastric gavage of GCA.
11. The rationale behind the test doses for BA-related agents in vivo and in vitro should be illustrated, and the method needs supplementation
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Zhao et al. demonstrated that GCA accumulates in the serum of patients with CRC. This accumulation leads to a reduced activity of the bile acid receptor FXR, resulting in a poor antitumor CD8+ T cell response. Mechanistically, GCA upregulates tumor PD-L1 expression through the FXR-SOX14-DHHC9 axis-mediated palmitoylation of PD-L1. While the study includes substantial experiments, it lacks novelty in terms of the role of GCA and its receptor in CRC and the palmitoylation of PD-L1 by DHHC9, as these have been reported in previous studies.
Major concerns:
1.The prediagnostic plasma GCA levels and colon cancer risk have already been reported (PMID: 31435679), as well as the mechanism regarding the role of DHHC9 on the expression of PD-L1 (PMID: 30514902). In addition, the bile acid receptor FXR agonist GW4064 has already been reported to enhance anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy in colorectal cancer (PMID: 37261088). Thus, the key points of this study are already known with less novelty.
2.The cluster identification by scRNA-seq in Figure 2 is not reasonable. The resolution seems very low and rough because no other myeloid clusters, such as dendritic cells, MDSCs, and neutrophils, or T-cell subsets (cytotoxic or exhausted), or tumor cells were found in the scRNA-seq. The cell population in scRNA-seq seems exactly the same as that found by flow cytometry. Especially, the macrophage population is the largest among tumor-infiltrating immune cells and is heterogeneous. What markers were used to identify the macrophages? No gene expression data were shown for each cluster.
3.Other independent cohorts or public databases should be analyzed to verify the clinical relevance between GCA and patient outcome. Are SOX14, GCA, and DHHC9 expression associated with patient survival in other studies? They should provide more evidence to validate their results.
4.Data quality is unsatisfactory. For example, all flow data of PD-L1 expression lack negative IgG control, such as Figure 2k, 2l, 3b, and 3g. The flow gating of exhausted T cells and interferon-gamma-producing T cells should be shown. Additionally, according to their method, why were the same colors used together (Tim-3-BV605 and PD1-BV605)?
5.In figures 4 and 6, all the in vivo mouse models are performed by subcutaneous injection. The tumor microenvironment differs significantly in different organs, so orthotopic models should be performed to validate the authors' conclusions.
Minor concerns:
6.What is the reason for the difference in GCA levels between healthy individuals and patients with CRC?
7.Macrophage depleted efficiency in Figure 2e should be detected.
8. Line 195 lacks a space.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This study shows that glycocholic acid (GCA) is associated with human colon cancer and that GCA promoted colon tumorigenesis in cultured colon cancer cell lines in immunocompetent xenograph mouse models through GCA inhibition of FXR signaling that altered the expression of target genes involved in immunomodulation of tumor growth by anti-PD-L1 and PD-1 drugs (such as nivolumab, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab, avelumab, aurvalumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab and retifanlimab). While FXR has been shown to be involved in repression of colon and liver cancer in a number of earlier studies, this is a novel mechanism if it can be substantiated by experimentation. The authors propose that this effect is a result of GCA antagonism of FXR. However, GCA has never been shown to be an FXR antagonist while TCA (taurine conjugate of CA), found in mice, is a potent FXR agonist. And others showed that GCA is an FXR activator. In the human colon cancer correlative study, it is not clear whether is the result of colon cancer or in increased by other means such as lower gut bacterial deconjugation leading to increased tumor grown and lower therapeutic efficacy of the anti-PD-L1 and PD-1 drugs. This seems to be a therapeutic story where activation of FXR could increase the anti-tumor response to anti-PD-L1 drugs. The mechanism of the anti-tumor effect is dependent on FXR expression in the tumor cells where the authors suggest that when FXR signaling is inhibited by GCA, it leads to PD-L1 palmitoylation via DHHC9 and PD-L1 stabilization. While the data are interesting and the effect of FXR agonist clear and convincing, the data on GCA as an FXR antagonist is not convincing and not in agreement with earlier studies.
Comments:
1. Figures 1 and 5: What are the concentrations of serum GCA in the low and high groups? What was the criteria for separating the low and high groups?
2. What is the concentration of GCA in human serum? Is this concentration of GCA sufficient to antagonized FXR in intestine and MC38, CT26, HCT116 and SW620 cell lines. The reference values for GCA in human serum are around <2.17 umol/ml (https://genetics.testcatalog.org/show/BAPS). This seems to be more than sufficient bind to and antagonize FXR signaling based on the concentration of GCA used in cultured cells 100 ng/ml (about 0.2 nmol/ml). This is why it is important to precisely know the GCA levels in the human “Low GCA” and “High GCA” groups in Figures 1 and 5. If the Low GCA group is higher than 0.2 nmol/ml, it is hard to argue that FXR is not being antagonized in high survival (Figure 1) and highly response to immunotherapy patients.
3. What is the concentration achieved in mice administered GCA (400 mg/kg p.o.) twice a week (from Figure 1 legend). A pharmacokinetic study should be done to determine if the serum levels obtained are withing the range of that found in humans and sufficient to modulate FXR in tumor cells.
4. FXR protein levels should be quantified in tumors of patients that are sensitive and resistant to anti-PD-L1 and anti-PD-1 monoclonal Ab drugs.
5. Mice are not a good model to study the effects of GCA since mice make trace amounts of GCA; they mostly make the taurine conjugate TCA. But they are a good model to study the therapeutic effects of GCA. This should be discussed.
6. GCA should be measured in CRC tumor tissues. In tumor tissues, are different GCA levels also correlative with FXR transcriptional activity and PD-L1 expression?
7. FXR silencing was found in tumor tissues by DNA methylation and KRAS signaling, hence cancer cells-induced xenograft is not proper for FXR inhibition studies (PMID: 24177031). FXR inhibition (GCA) studies should be done in WT and FXR-KO AOM/DSS-induced CRC models.
8. The authors should verify their main findings in the AOM/DSS induced CRC mouse models or in human CRC organoids. Are Fxr-null mice more resistant than wild-type mice to anti-PD-L1 therapy?
9. Quantitative western blots should be performed on wild-type and FXR knockout MC38, CT26, HCT116 and SW620 cells. In all experiments suing GCA, typical FXR tart genes mRNAs should be measured.
10. Most of the experiments were performed in xenograft models, but the authors did not include FXR-KO in all the xenograft models. What is the tumor growth of FXR-knockout/knockdown cancer cells? GCA/TβMCA/GW4064 treatment should be done in both WT and FXR-KO cancer cells-injected xenograft models.
11. GCA has never been shown to be an FXR antagonist. However, earlier studies found that GCA is an FXR agonist (See Figure 5 in PMID: 16230354). In addition, TCA is a potent FXR agonist (PMID: 23051670). What is the explanation for this stark difference between the results in this study and the earlier published data? In silico modeling studies should be done to explain why GCA antagonizes FXR while TCA activates FXR.
12. As reviewed in PMID: 23603607 and PMID: 28249269, IBABP (FABP6) and ASBT (SLC10A2), respectively, are required for bile acid (FXR ligands) uptake into cells. Do MC38, CT26, HCT116 and SW620 cells express biologically significant levels of IBABP and ASBT? This should be determined by western blots. Tumor cells frequently lose expression of many genes and transporters found in normal colon/intestinal epithelial cells that not required for cell growth.
13. I am not aware of any studies in nuclear receptors where an antagonist inhibits RXR dimerization to repress transcription. Most studies found that nuclear receptor antagonist bind to the ligand-binding site and inhibits the recruitment of transcriptional co-activators and/or recruit transcriptional co-repressors. Based on many years of FXR studies, the most likely explanation for GCA antagonist activity is that it displaces FXR agonist. The authors need to perform more definitive studies to show the mechanism by which GCA suppresses FXR signaling. Since the authors stated that GCA is a novel antagonist/inhibitor of FXR with a totally novel inhibition pattern, more structure-based evidence should be offered. Does GCA directly bind to FXR? What’s the binding site? How this GCA-FXR binding influence its activity?
14. The studies showing increase in tumor growth in the xenograph MC38, CT26, HCT116 and SW620 cell lines and in the AOM-DSS mouse model should be done using a confirmed FXR antagonist (PMID: 33995909) given the concerns about whether GCA is a bona fide FXR antagonist.
15. Guo and colleagues published in 2009 (PMID: 18981289) that inhibition/loss of intestinal FXR results in increase colon tumorigenesis, thus diminishing the novelty of this study. This paper should be cited and discussed.
16. Others have shown that FXR agonist suppress colon cancer (PMID: 33436792). This paper should be cited and discussed.
17. A number of papers have shown a role for bile acids in colon cancer (PMID: 30794774; PMID: 36765047). Notably, the gut microbiota, bile acids, and intestinal FXR signaling have been shown to influence colon cancer in mouse models of CRC. These papers and other relevant to the present study should be cited and discussed.
18. It was reported that activation of FXR inhibited intestinal cancer stem cell proliferation and alleviated CRC progression (PMID: 30794774). However, the authors found that FXR did not influence the growth rate of cancer cells. This inconsistent conclusion should be discussed.
Minor comments:
19. What was the method for measuring bile acid concentration in humans and mice? Were standards used to precisely quantify the bile acid metabolites?
20. Fxr floxed mice were purchased from Cyagen Biosciences, Inc. (cat. no. S-CKO- 555 04890). To my knowledge, this mouse line has never been published and there is no data showing that the intestinal epithelial-specific Fxr knockout (Fxrko) mice lack FXR expression in intestinal epithelial cells.
