• Units of the heatmap in panel A is not defined (z-scores?)
• Panels B/C: y-axis label is misspelled (should be ‘concentration’)
• Panels B/C: concentration units are not defined either in the figure or in the caption
• Panels B/C: if the revised GCA concentrations shown are simply transformed from the original log2 values (now linear), the
values do not seem to match up. For example, in panel B of the original manuscript, the range for stage I-II tumors is roughly 6.3-
6.8 in log2 units, which corresponds to ~ 79-111 linear units as shown in the revised manuscript. However, while the range for
stage III-IV tumors in the original manuscript of ~ 6.5-6.85 should correspond to ~ 91-115 in linear units, the numbers shown in
the revised manuscript for this group are considerably higher, lending the impression of much larger differences between tumor
stages. The data for panel C are similarly discordant between manuscript versions (upper range of M0 group and the entire range
of M1 is too high in revised version). The authors should explain this discrepancy and check the presented data for accuracy.
• Panels D-E: authors should include information on the cutoff used for high vs low GCA and the sample size should be
specified for each group, either in the figures or in legends. Same suggestion applies to KM curves in supplementary figures.
A: We thank the reviewer for the careful evaluation and insightful comments.
Panel A (Heatmap):
We apologize for not defining the units in the heatmap. The heatmap in Panel A represents z-scores. This has now been clarified
in both the figure legend and the revised manuscript text.
Panels B/C:
We sincerely apologize for the confusion caused by the discrepancy in values of serum GCA concentration between the original
and revised versions of Panels B and C. In our original manuscript, the log2 values on the y-axis reflected relative expression levels
of serum GCA in CRC patients compared to healthy individuals. These were not absolute concentrations.
In the revised version, Panels B and C now display the absolute serum GCA concentrations (in nM) without transformation. We
have re-verified the dataset to ensure the accuracy of these values. The apparent mismatch between transformed and linear values
was due to the change in data representation, not a computational error. To avoid further confusion, we have updated the y-axis
labels to correctly read “GCA concentration (nM)” and corrected the spelling of “concentration” in both Panels B and C.
Panels D-E and Kaplan-Meier Curves
We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. The cutoff for high vs. low GCA groups was determined based on the mean value of the
dataset. We have now included this information in the figure legends for Panels D-E and all Kaplan–Meier curves in revised Figures.
All changes have been incorporated into the revised manuscript.
2. Association of serum GCA concentrations with patient survival:
In my previous comments, I made the following suggestion: It would be interesting/informative to compare BA concentrations in
patients with liver vs non-liver metastases and include liver metastasis specifically as a covariate in survival analysis (as distinct
from other metastatic sites)
The authors have evaluated a larger (n=308) CRC cohort in an effort to address this question but concluded that the number of
patients with liver metastasis (35 with liver only) is too small to enable robust conclusions. I agree that the small number of liver
mets in this cohort is statistically limiting and makes it difficult to draw conclusions about the liver met+ patient segment. However,
the authors could additionally evaluate the relationship between PFS/OS and serum BA in patients without metastasis—if a PFS/OS
association is observed in patients with earlier stage disease, it would increase confidence that the clinical observations are
independent of liver metastasis.
A: We thank the reviewer for the insightful follow-up suggestion. In response, we have performed additional survival analyses
focusing on colorectal cancer (CRC) patients with documented disease-free survival (DFS) and no evidence of liver metastases (n
= 247) to assess the association between serum GCA concentrations and clinical outcomes. Kaplan–Meier analyses demonstrated
that higher serum GCA concentrations remained significantly associated with both shorter disease-free survival (DFS) and overall
survival (OS) in this subgroup. These results reinforce our original observation that elevated serum GCA levels are linked to poor
clinical outcomes in CRC and suggest that this association is independent of the presence of liver metastases (Fig.SS1, original
Fig.S1G-H).
Fig. SS1. (A, B) Disease-free survival (A, DFS) and overall survival (B, OS) curves for 247 colorectal cancer (CRC) patients
without liver metastases in cohort II. Patients were stratified based on the mean serum glycocholic acid (GCA) concentration as
the cut-off value.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
After reviewing the revised manuscript, I am pleased to note that the authors have effectively addressed all the concerns raised.
The revisions have significantly enhanced the quality of the paper. I do not have any further questions or concerns at this time.
A: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful feedback and kind words. We are grateful for the constructive suggestions
throughout the review process, which have greatly improved the quality and clarity of our manuscript.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
I appreciate the revisions to the manuscript resubmitted by the authors. With new experiments they have addressed many of
my concerns. Nevertheless, I still have the following concerns:
A: We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the revisions and additional experiments we have performed. Below, we address the
remaining concerns point by point.
1. This manuscript demonstrates limited novelty, particularly regarding the clinical role of GW4064 in immunotherapy and the
regulatory mechanisms of PD-L1.
A: We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the novelty of our findings. While it has been previously reported that FXR
agonist GW4064 enhances anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy efficacy in CRC (Lu et al., Oncoimmunology, 2023), our study offers
additional mechanistic and translational insights that we believe add novel value to the field.
Bile acids (BAs) play a dual role in regulating tumorigenesis, and different bile acid species exert distinct effects. Recent studies
have provided emerging evidence that several BAs, including deoxycholic acid (DCA) and lithocholic acid (LCA), are critical for
shaping tumor microenvironment to induce tumor evasion (Cong et al., Immunity, 2024; Varanasi et al., Science, 2025). Therefore,
distinguishing among BA species and elucidating their mechanism of regulating tumor-TME crosstalk is essential.
In our study, we identify GCA not only as a pre-diagnostic serum biomarker but also as a functional driver of colorectal
tumorigenesis, acting through the SOX14/DHHC9/PD-L1 axis. We further demonstrate that GCA promotes PD-L1 stability via
FXR inhibition and downstream transcriptional activation of SOX14 and DHHC9, providing a previously unrecognized
mechanistic link between FXR signaling and PD-L1 palmitoylation.
Moreover, we show that combined treatment with GW4064 and anti-PD-1 antibody effectively suppresses tumor growth even in
anti-PD-1–resistant CRC models and in mice with elevated GCA levels. These findings not only support and extend prior
observations but also broaden the therapeutic applicability of FXR agonist-based immunotherapy, particularly in GCA-enriched
CRC subsets. We believe this mechanistic and translational depth offers meaningful innovation beyond previously published work.
2. Representative orthotopic tumor images should be presented to support the efficacy of GCA treatment on indicated groups in
Fig. S15.
A: Thank you for this helpful suggestion. We believe there may have been a reference error, as Figure S15 was not included in our
revised manuscript. We assume the reviewer intended to refer to Figures S1–5, which present data on the efficacy of GCA treatment.
In response, we have now included representative tumor images from the indicated experimental groups in the revised Figure S1-
5, to visually support the quantitative tumor burden data. We believe this addition provides stronger visual evidence of treatment
efficacy. These images were integrated in the in Supplementary Figure 13 (Fig.S13) of the revised manuscript.
3. The quality of the figures requires further improvement. For example, scale bars are absent from the immunofluorescence images
in Fig. 5B. Molecular weight markers are not labeled on each Western blot result.
A: We appreciate the reviewer’s comments and have made the following revisions to improve figure quality throughout the
manuscript. Scale bars have been added to “Merge” panel of Fig. 5B. Molecular weight markers have been labeled on each blot to
indicate protein size.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
THe response to the reviewers are incomplete.
Q1&2. There is no evidence that GCA as an FXR antagonist as established in many earlier studies. This critical issue is not
addressed. GCA and other derived bile acids in serum and tumor tissues should be measured after GCA administration in vivo.
What are the median concentrations of GCA in cohort 1 and cohort 2? Is it above 100 µM or below 100 µM? As shown in figure
SS10C, there was no dose effect on FXR inhibition when GCA concentration was 100 µM or more.
A: We sincerely thank the reviewer for these insightful and detailed comments and acknowledge the reviewer’s important point
regarding the mechanistic classification of GCA.
1. On GCA as an FXR antagonist:
We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern that the classification of GCA as an FXR antagonist remains a matter of ongoing
investigation. While previous reports have demonstrated that GCA can inhibit FXR activity in human cancer cells (Dai et al.,
Journal of Hematology & Oncology, 2011), there is limited direct evidence establishing this function at physiological
concentrations in vivo. Accordingly, we do not assert that GCA acts as a classical pharmacological antagonist. Instead, our data
suggests that GCA exposure is associated with reduced FXR activity in CRC, as indicated by downregulation of canonical FXR
target genes (e.g., Shp, Fgf15) and concomitant increases in PD-L1 expression.
2. On bile acid concentrations in vivo (serum and tumor):
Regarding the in vivo GCA treatment, we agree that endogenous and systemic bile acid levels are critical to interpreting the data.
As suggested, we measured the concentrations of GCA and other bile acids, specifically TDCA, TCA, TCDCA, GCDCA, and
GDCA, which are significantly elevated in the serum of CRC patients compared to healthy individuals (Fig.1A), following GCA
administration (400 mg/kg) in a subcutaneous MC38 tumor model. Consistent with previous reports, serum GCA levels were barely
detectable in healthy mice or in tumor-bearing mice without GCA treatment. In contrast, several serum levels of other bile acids
were elevated in MC38 tumor-bearing mice relative to healthy controls. Of note, a detectable accumulation of serum GCA
approximately 150 nM was observed in serum of mice receiving GCA treatment. In tumor tissues, GCA levels remained low in
mice untreated, while the concentration was measurable, with a concentration of approximately 82 nmol/g in GCA-treated tumors
(Fig.SS2A, B, original Fig.S3C, D).
As shown in Figure SS10C of our previous response, we treated cultured cells with 1 mL of complete DMEM containing 100 nM
(100 nmol/L) GCA. We have carefully reviewed our data and apologize for the earlier labeling error, where "100 μM" (equivalent
to 100 nmol/mL) was mistakenly used instead of the correct "100 nM" (100 nmol/L), due to a unit conversion issue. At and above
100 nM GCA-treatment in vitro, we observed effective FXR inhibition, evidenced by reduced FXRE-luciferase reporter activity
in treated cells compared to untreated controls (Fig.S2B).
Importantly, the median GCA concentration in mouse serum after GCA treatment (157.48 nM) falls within the range that has been
shown to inhibit FXR signaling under experimental conditions (100-200nM). Furthermore, the median serum GCA concentrations
in our human cohorts were approximately 96.4 nM in Cohort 1 and 96.7 nM in Cohort 2. These values are comparable to or slightly
lower than those observed in GCA-treated mice and in vitro cultures, supporting the physiological relevance of our experimental
models.
Fig. SS2. (A, B) The serum (A) or tumoral (B) concentration of indicated BAs in healthy mice or mice inoculated with MC38 cells
following indicated GCA treatment (400mg/kg, n=6).
3. Although there is sufficient data showing that FXR signaling was suppressed in mice treated with 400 mg/kg GCA, it is unknown
whether the serum levels of GCA obtained under this treatment is within the range of that found in humans, which is very important
to determine the translational value of this study.
A: We appreciate the reviewer’s important point regarding the translational relevance of the GCA dosing used in our mouse model.
As outlined above, we have now quantified serum GCA concentrations in mice treated with 400 mg/kg GCA. The median GCA
level was approximately 157.48 nM, which is slightly higher than the median serum GCA concentrations (~100nM) observed in
CRC patients.
Thus, the serum GCA levels achieved in our mouse model are not only comparable to those in human CRC patients but also fall
within the same order of magnitude. This concordance supports the translational relevance of our dosing regimen. Importantly, the
observed suppression of FXR signaling and associated immunological changes in GCA-treated mice occurred at physiologically
relevant concentrations, further underscoring the clinical significance of our findings.
8. To determine if Fxr-null mice are more resistant than WT mice to anti-PD-L1 therapy, four groups of mice are needed, i.e. WT
vehicle, WT anti-PD-L1, Fxr null vehicle, Fxr null anti-PD-L1. In addition to the comparisons between WT and Fxr null mice,
like the authors had done in Figure SS19, the comparisons between vehicle and anti-PD-L1 groups are needed to evaluate the effect of
anti-PD-L1 treatment. In fact, if you compare the data in Figure SS18 and Figure SS19, there was almost no improvement in tumor
number and tumor area between FXR WT mock group and FXR WT anti-PD-L1 group, suggesting that WT mice were almost
completely resistant to anti-PD-L1 therapy.
A: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive comment. We fully agree that evaluating the effect of anti-PD-L1
therapy requires the inclusion of all four groups: Fxrwt + IgG, Fxrwt + anti-PD-L1, Fxr-/- + IgG, and Fxr-/- + anti-PD-L1, to allow
direct comparisons both within and between genotypes.
In our study, we utilized Fxr-knockout (Fxr-/-) and their littermate wild-type (Fxrwt) controls in the AOM/DSS-induced CRC model
to assess the response to anti-PD-L1 treatment. While the comparisons of tumor number and tumor area in mice between Fxrwt
mock group of Figure SS18 and Fxrwt anti-PD-1α group of Figure SS19 did not appear significantly different in our previous
responses, it is important to note that these data were derived from independent experiments, and minor discrepancies could be due
to biological variability between mouse batches or age ranges.
In our repeated experiments using four groups, we observed that anti-PD-L1 treatment at dosage of 10mg/kg significantly reduced
tumor burden in Fxrwt mice, indicating a robust response to therapy in the WT background. More importantly, anti-PD-L1 therapy
in Fxr-/- mice resulted in marked acceleration in both tumor number and tumor area, as well as shorter colon length, compared to
Fxrwt mice receiving the same treatment (Fig.SS3, original Fig.S7J). This reduction of therapeutic efficacy in Fxr-deficient mice
underscores our central conclusion: Fxr-deficiency inhibits the response of the tumor microenvironment to PD-1/PD-L1 immune
checkpoint blockade.
Fig.SS3. Fxr-knockout mice (Fxr-/-) and their litter mates (Fxrwt) were injected with anti-PD-L1 antibody (10mg/kg) or IgG (i.g.)
during AOM/DSS treatment (n=6 per group). Colon length (left), tumor numbers (middle) and tumor areas (right) of colons were
shown.
21. This question is about the source of the villin-cre mice, not the background of this mouse strain. Is this mouse strain from the
Jackson Lab, or other sources? This should be clarified in the manuscript.
A: We apologize for the omission of this detail. In the revised manuscript (Materials and Methods), we have clarified that:
Villin-Cre (#004586) transgenic mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME, USA) to create conditional
knockout mice and silenced the expression of Fxr in intestinal epithelial cells.
The responses to the comments point by point:
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have effectively addressed the concerns previously raised. I have no further questions or suggestions at this time.
A: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their positive evaluation of our revisions. We are pleased that our additional experiments
and analyses have satisfactorily addressed the previous concerns. We greatly appreciate the reviewer’s constructive feedback
throughout the review process, which has helped us improve the quality and clarity of the manuscript.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have effectively addressed the concerns previously raised. I have no further questions or suggestions at this time.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The responses to the comments point by point:
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author): with expertise in cancer immunology,
colorectal cancer
Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a highly prevalent tumor type that is generally refractory to
immunotherapy. Thus, elucidating mechanisms of CRC resistance to immunotherapy is
of high importance. In this study, Zhao et al make use of a comprehensive range of
clinical data, in vivo models, and in vitro cell biology assays to identify bile acids as
potential regulators of CRC sensitivity to T cell attack. Mechanistically, this is proposed
to occur through the bile acid nuclear receptor Fxr, which regulates expression of
SOX14 and the palmitoyltransferase DHHC9 to control palmitoylation and stability of
the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1. Overall, the experiments appear to have been
generally well-executed (although the methodological details are not always clear, nor
is it clear how often experiments were reproduced). The connection between bile-
acid/Fxr-dependent regulation of tumor PD-L1 expression is not well understood in the
context of CRC, but a similar set of observations were recently published for
hepatocellular carcinoma (Gong et al, Front Oncol, 2021).
Overall, the data are interesting and shed light on a mechanism of PD-L1 regulation
that is not well understood. However, I have several concerns that should be addressed
prior to publication.
We thank the reviewer for his/her positive comments on our paper and have addressed
all the questions raised by the reviewer as outlined below.
Major concerns:
1. Fig. 1b/c: GCA concentrations are noted on the y-axis as ‘relative concentration’, but
what are they relative to? The median differences between early and late-stage disease
(panel B) or localized vs metastatic disease (panel C) may be statistically significant
but are less than 0.1 in log2 space, which equates to a <7% difference. Are this
difference considered biologically or clinically meaningful? Is it possible to estimate
bile acid concentrations in tumor tissue?
R: We appreciate the reviewer’s careful reading of our manuscript and apologize for
not clearly describing this point in our first version of the manuscript and any confusion
it might have caused. It is our mistake, we have deleted “relative” in the revised
manuscript; we also re-analyzed the serum GCA levels by using GCA concentration
and showed in Fig. 1B, C of revised manusript.
As pointed out by the reviewer, the differences of GCA concentration in CRC
patients with early- and late-stage or localized vs. metastatic disease CRC appears
marginal. Similar observations have been reported in other study, where serum GCA
concentration showed only marginal changes between early- and late-stage patients
with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (J Cancer Res Clin Oncol. 2023
Dec;149(19):17285-17296). In our study, we only recruit 80 CRC patients (Cohort 1)
initially; we have added another cohort of CRC patients (308 patients in total, Cohort
2) in our revised manuscript. Our new data also demonstrated that high serum GCA
concentration not only was positively related with advanced tumor stage but also
predict poor overall survival and disease-free survival. We have updated these results
in our manuscript (Fig. SS1A-D, original Figure Fig. S1C-F).
Bile acids are released into the small intestine in response to cholecystokinin
stimulus upon meal ingestion. In the gut lumen, bile acids facilitate transport, digestion
and absorption of nutrients, particularly lipids and lipid-soluble vitamins. Up to 95 %
of bile acids are actively re-absorbed in the terminal ileum and transported back to the
liver and enter the systemic circulation. it has been suggested that blood levels of bile
acids could be more useful to investigate associations with cancer risk than fecal bile
acids, and small case-control studies have found increased serum bile acids levels in
patients with colon cancer. We have previously evaluated the concentrations of bile acid
(BA) concentrations in tumor tissue from small samples, the concentrations were very
low, thus we did not show these data and chose the blood levels of bile acids for further
study.
Fig. SS1. (A) Serum GCA levels in stages I-II (n=117) and III-IV patients (n=191) with
CRC (n=308, Cohort 2). (B) Serum GCA levels in patients with CRC patients with
metastatic disease (M1, n=59) or without metastatic disease (M0, n=249). (C and D)
Kaplan-Meier analyses with log-rank test were used to evaluate Disease-free survival
(C) and overall survival (D) of 308 CRC patients based on their serum GCA levels
using the median GCA levels as cut-off value.
2. Fig. 1d/e and Fig. S1a/b: elevated circulating bile acid concentrations are typically
associated with hepatic dysfunction (resulting in impaired clearance of bile acids from
portal blood). This raises the question of whether the increased GCA concentrations
observed in patients with metastatic CRC are due to liver metastases impairing hepatic
function (as opposed to a causative role of GCA in promoting CRC progression, as
implied in this manuscript). It would be interesting/informative to compare BA
concentrations in patients with liver vs non-liver metastases and include liver metastasis
specifically as a covariate in survival analysis (as distinct from other metastatic sites).
R: We appreciate the reviewer's insightful question regarding the potential impact of
liver metastases on circulating bile acid concentrations and their association with CRC
progression. In our initial study, we only recruit 80 cancer patients and only few patients
with liver metastasis, thus we did not compare BA concentrations in patients with liver
vs non-liver metastases and include liver metastasis. In the new 308 CRC patients’
cohort, 39 patients were diagnosed with liver metastases (35 patients with only liver
metastasis and 4 patients had liver and other organ metastasis). We found that the mean
serum GCA concentrations, were significantly increased in the CRC patients with liver-
metastases compared to those without liver-metastasis (Fig. SS2A-D). Kaplan-Meier
survival analyses with log-rank test showed that no significant difference was found
between high and low GCA concentration patients’ overall survival who had only liver
metastasis, although there were poor trend for high GCA level’s patients (Fig. SS2A-
D). This might be caused by small samples. Whether high GCA could affect the liver
metastasis and the specific mechanism need more detailed explorations, we will
conduct another study in future. Thus, we did not supplement these results in our revised
manuscript.
Fig. SS2. (A). Different GCA concentrations in patients with all 39-liver vs non-liver
metastases(n=269) among CRC patients of Cohort 2. (B) Different GCA concentrations
in patients with only liver(n=35) vs non-liver metastases(n=269) among CRC patients
of Cohort 2. (C and D) Kaplan-Meier analyses with log-rank test were used to evaluate
overall survival in patients with liver metastasis and other metastasis (C) and in patients
with only liver metastasis (D) among Cohort 2’s CRC patients.
3. Fig. 1f/h/i (DSS-AOM data): the DSS-AOM model data are intriguing, but somewhat
challenging to interpret. The DSS-AOM regimen models colitis-associated CRC, which
follows a distinct process of pathogenesis compared to the much more common
sporadic CRCs (which are the principal focus of this manuscript). Most importantly,
tumorigenesis in this system relies on repeated rounds of DSS-driven colitis, and tumor
burden is associated with the severity of DSS-driven tissue damage. Because the
authors appear to have used mice with constitutive loss of Fxr in intestinal epithelial
cells (Fxr.flox crossed with Villin-Cre), it is not possible based on these data to
determine whether Fxr function is associated with alterations in tumorigenesis, colitis,
or both. One potential alternative is to use mice with inducible Villin-controlled Cre
(Vill. Cre. ERT2) so that Fxr can be deleted in colon epithelial cells after the final round
of DSS (to exclude effects on colitis). However, the challenge of interpreting colitis-
associated CRC data in the context of a paper that's focused on sporadic CRC remains.
If the authors' intent is simply to generate data using an orthotopic model of CRC,
alternative systems could include direct implantation of CRC cell lines into colon
mucosa, or delivery of CRC cells to the liver via hydrodynamic tail vein injection.
R: The reviewer’s concern is thoughtful. Following your kind suggestion, we generated
an orthotopic mice model of CRC by implanting MC38 tumors into colon mucosa. This
approach provides a more relevant model for studying sporadic CRC and allows us to
focus specifically on the role of FXR in tumorigenesis without the confounding effects
of colitis associated with the DSS-AOM model. In brief, wild-type 10-12 weeks old
C57BL/6 mice were examined by endoscopy to ensure the colonic mucosa was healthy
prior to implantation after anesthesia. For tumor cell implantation, 0.5×106 Fxr-
knockout (sg FXR) MC38 cells or control cells (sg CON) diluted in 50 μL of PBS were
injected very slowly towards the lumen of lower mid and distal colon ~30 mm from the
anal verge to induce tumor growth by using endoscopic injection. Consistently, the
growth of Fxr-KO MC38 tumors by using this orthotopic mice model of CRC was
significantly increased compared to that of control tumors (Fig. SS3A, original Figure
Fig. S3A). In addition, a worse overall survival was observed in mice with Fxr-KO
MC38 tumors compared to those with controls (Fig. SS3B, original Figure Fig. S3A),
which further confirmed our conclusion that FXR inhibits CRC tumorigenesis.
Fig. SS3. (A-B) 0.5×106 indicated MC38 cells were endoscopy-guided injected into the
lumen of lower mid and distal colon ~30 mm from the anal verge of C57BL/6J mice
(n=5). (A)Tumor volumes and (B)mortality within the observation period of the
indicated mice were shown. All the experiments were repeated three times. The results
are presented as the mean ± SD.
4. Treatment with GCA apparently reduces activity of FXRE significantly in the
luciferase reporter system (cell line assays). What is the source of the basal reporter
signal? Is this an overexpression artifact, or are the cells exposed to bile acids in culture
medium (possibly via serum)?
R: We understand the reviewer’s point. In our study, CRC cells were cultured in DMEM
supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS). To investigate whether serum
contributes to the basal activity of FXR signaling, we cultured MC38 cells transfected
with FXRE reporter system in DMEM supplemented with or without 10% FBS and
observed that luciferase activity was significantly upregulated in cells with FBS
compared to that in plain DMED (Fig. SS4). Our experiment provided clear evidence
that the basal FXR signaling activity in our luciferase assays is due to the presence of
FBS in the culture medium, which was crucial for interpreting the effects of GCA on
FXR activity.
Fig. SS4. MC38 cells transfected with reporter plasmids linked to an FXR-responsive
element (FXRE-Luc) were cultured in plain DMEM for 24h, followed cultured with
10% FBS DMEM (Normal) or plain DMEM (Plain) for another 24h. Luciferase activity
of MC38 cells was shown (n=5).
5. Figure 2I: The authors report that treatment of MC38 cells with GCA significantly
induced PDL1 expression at the protein level, but not at the mRNA level. PDL1 is well-
known to be an interferon-inducible gene, and it is noteworthy that several other
proteins identified by the authors as induced by GCA are also known to be interferon-
inducible, including Ifi204, B2m, Mndal, and H2-M3. Is this merely a coincidence, or
is it possible that GCA-treatment is inducing an autocrine type I IFN response?
Have
the authors performed an unbiased transcriptional analysis (e.g. bulk RNAseq) to
determine if such an interferon-like response is indeed occurring?
R: This is a thoughtful question. In our study, we made an intriguing observation that
GCA did not affect the expression of interferon-stimulated genes in vitro (original
Figure Fig.S5H). Of note, the mRNA level of PD-L1 was not altered in cells treated
with GCA, suggesting that GCA-mediated upregulation of PD-L1 is not dependent on
interferon signaling (original Figure Fig.S6E). To further validate our results, we
measured the transcriptional level of type I interferon (IFNα and IFNβ), transcriptional
factors of IFN, including STAT1, STAT2, IRF1, IRF2, IRF5 and interferon-stimulated
gene 15 (ISG15), essential for cellular IFN signaling transduction in GCA- or GW4064-
treated MC38 and HCT116 CRC cells. However, functionally suppression or activation
of FXR signaling in CRC cells did not alter the mRNA level of IFNs or ISGs (Fig.SS5).
Our data suggested that GCA does not affect IFN-response in vitro.
Fig. SS5.qRT-PCR measurement of the expression of indicated mRNA in MC38 (left)
and HCT116 (right) cells treated with GCA or GW4064 for 24h. (B) GSEA analysis of
type I IFN response in MC38 cells treated with or without GCA for 24 h based on RNA-
sequencing.
6. Fig. S4H/I: the apparent dependency of Fxr-driven tumor growth effects on tumor
PDL1 expression is interesting and important to the overall message of the paper. To
exclude the possibility that this phenotype is driven by clone-to-clone differences, can
this observation be further supported by blocking PDL1 in tumors from wild type cells
(e.g. with anti-PD-L1 blocking antibody) in the presence or absence of Fxr ligands?
R: Follow your kind suggesting, we used a subcutaneous wild-type MC38 or CT26
tumor model to address this question. In brief, we subcutaneously injected 0.5×106
MC38 or CT26 cells diluted in 100 μL of PBS in the right flank of C57BL/6 or BALB/c
mice to induce tumor growth, respectively. Mice were treated with GCA (400 mg/kg
p.o.) and/or anti-PD-L1 (10mg/kg and 100mg/kg) twice a week at day 10 post injection.
Similarly, the results showed that functional impairment of FXR by GCA in CRC cells
significantly promoted the growth of tumors. While low dose anti-PD-L1 therapy
(10mg/kg), which was sufficiently prevent the growth of MC38 and CT26 tumors in
mice under normal condition, did not inhibit the development of tumors in mice with
GCA (Fig. SS6 A-B, original Fig.S7H-I), suggesting that 50mg/kg of anti-PD-L1
antibody might not fully neutralizing PD-L1 in tumor microenvironment (TME). Of
note, blocking PD-L1/PD-1-signaling by treatment of high dose of anti-PD-L1
(100mg/kg) was sufficiently reverted GCA-induced tumorigenesis (Fig. SS4 A-B),
which further confirming our results that PD-L1 expression in tumors was critical for
FXR-mediated tumor suppression.
Fig. SS6. (A-B) C57BL/6 (n=6) or BALB/c mice inoculated with MC38 (A) or CT26
(B) tumor cells were treated with GCA (o.p) twice a week and/or with anti-PD-L1
antibody or IgG 7 days post injection. The tumor volumes (left) and weights (right) are
shown.
7. Figure 5: the authors propose that the Fxr-regulated SOX14/DHH-C9/PD-L1 axis is
involved in resistance of MSI-H/dMMR CRC patients to anti-PD-1 therapy in the clinic.
This conclusion seems potentially odd—if we assume that tumor-expressed PD-L1 acts
by engaging PD-1 on T cells, and if the anti-PD-1 antibody (the specific identity of the
treatment regimen should be stated in methods) was dosed adequately to fully inhibit
PD-1, then why would increase expression of PD-L1 on tumor cells have any bearing
on anti-PD-1 response? Is there any reason to believe that these patients did NOT
receive a dose of anti-PD-1 sufficient for full target coverage?
R: We appreciate this insightful question Although ICB therapy has durable effects
toward a subset of microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) CRCs, accounting for ~15%
of all CRC cases, only 30-50% of these patients can benefit from this therapy. Anti-PD-

8. Figure 6 (and various associated statements in text): along a similar line, the authors

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Serum bile acids (BAs) emerge as risk factors for cancer, but their roles in colorectal cancer (CRC) remain unclear.
We show that glycocholic acid (GCA), a primary BA, is elevated in the serum of CRC patients. In a mouse CRC
model, GCA promotes tumor programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression in tumors, suppressing CD8⁺ T cell-
mediated antitumor immunity and facilitating tumor growth. Mechanistically, GCA inhibits the BA receptor farnesoid
X receptor (FXR), a transcriptional repressor for SRY-box transcription factor 14 (SOX14). Loss of FXR repression
upregulates SOX14-mediated expression of zinc finger DHHC-type palmitoyl transferase 9 (DHHC9), thereby
reducing PD-L1 palmitoylation and stabilization. Silencing SOX14 or DHHC9, or activating FXR, synergizes with
anti-PD-1 therapy, reducing tumor growth in GCA-treated mice. These findings uncover a mechanism that GCA
remodels the tumor microenvironment to mediate CRC resistance to immunotherapy, highlighting therapeutic
opportunities targeting the FXR-PD-L1 axis in CRC patients with elevated serum GCA.

---

## Introduction

Colorectal cancer (CRC) represents one of the main causes of mortality.1, 2 Previous studies have shown that
programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)-expressing tumor cells attenuate CD8+ T cell infiltration, which results in tumor
progression.3 Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies, including anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-
1)/PD-L1 or anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 therapies, have changed the therapeutic landscape and
provided an unprecedented clinical response in various types of cancer.3, 4, 5 Although ICB therapy has durable effects
toward a subset of microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) CRCs, accounting for ~15% of all CRC cases, only 30-50%
of these patients can benefit from this therapy.6 Regrettably, patients with microsatellite instability stable
(MSS)/proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) (~85%) merely have a 5-10% response rate. Metabolic reprogramming
contributes to tumor immune evasion and progression, which is also considered as an important hallmark in tumors.
It has been shown that metabolic reprogramming in CRC regulated by cholesterol or fatty acids is sufficient to reshape
the tumor microenvironment (TME), leading to resistance towards ICB therapy.7, 8, 9, 10 Therefore, the identification of
key metabolites in regulating resistance to PD-L1 therapy is necessary to combat an immunosuppressive TME in CRC.

The expression of PD-L1 in tumor cells is regulated by various processes, including transcription and post-
transcriptional modifications (PTMs).11 During cell malignant transformation and tumor initiation, the transcription
level of PD-L1 is associated with oncogenic pathways such as aberrant activation of WNT/β-catenin and RAS/MAPK
signaling.12, 13 Moreover, PATMs, including palmitoylation, are critical for regulating the protein stability and function
of PD-L1, and consequentially leading to reduced anti-tumor immunity in the TME. 14 It has been demonstrated that
metabolic stress alters palmitoyl transferase-induced protein palmitoylation.14, 15 Notably, the palmitoyl transferases
zinc finger DHHC-type palmitoyl transferase (DHHC)3 and DHHC9 have been reported as key regulators for
mediating the palmitoylation of PD-L1, which contributes to lysosome sorting during PD-L1 degradation in several
types of cancer.14, 16 Thus, to identify whether and how metabolic alterations in CRC regulate the effects of PD-L1
palmitoylation is important for improving ICB therapy.

Bile acids (BAs) are considered as important regulators of intestinal epithelial homeostasis in the gastrointestinal tract.
In addition to their detergent properties,17 BAs serve as ligands to nuclear (hormone) receptors such as the farnesoid
X receptor (FXR), thus controlling numerous important cellular metabolism, regulatory and signaling functions, as
well as immune responses.18 In CRC, circulating levels of BAs are strongly associated with tumor initiation and
progression.19, 20 However, activation of FXR negatively regulates intestinal cancer stem cell proliferation, leading to
a slower CRC progression.21 Therefore, the role of BAs in regulating tumor initiation and development is still
controversial, and it remains unknown whether alterations in BAs-mediated signaling in tumor cells may affect
immune surveillance and ICB sensitivity.

The present study demonstrated that FXR inactivation mediated by the serum primary BA glycocholic acid (GCA) in
CRC is necessary and sufficient to inhibit the antitumor response of CD8+ T cells. Mechanistically, GCA increased
the expression of the transcription factor (TF) SRY-box transcription factor 14 (SOX14) by inhibiting FXR
transcription-suppressing function, and consequentially promoted the DHHC9-induced palmitoylation and
stabilization of PD-L1. Notably, activation of FXR with the agonist GW4064 sensitized ICB-resistant CRC to anti-
PD-1/PD-L1 treatment. Taken together, the present findings indicate that targeting the FXR signaling pathway is a
potential strategy for alleviating immunosuppressive TME and enhancing the sensitivity to anti-PDL-1 treatment in
CRC.

---

## Results

Increased serum GCA in patients with CRC is associated with poor clinical prognosis. It has been suggested that
the elevation of serum BAs is associated with higher risk for multiple cancer types22, however, the association between
BAs and CRC remains to be elucidated. To investigate whether BAs and which BA is associated with CRC
tumorigenesis, we collected serum samples from 80 patients with CRC (Cohort1) and 20 healthy individuals, and
measured the levels of 33 kinds of BAs including primary free, secondary free, primary conjugated and secondary
conjugated BAs by ultra performance LC-MS. It was found that only 6 BAs, that is, glycocholic acid (GCA),
taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TDCA), taurocholic acid (TCA), taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA),
glycochenodeoxycholic acid (GCDCA) and glycodeoxycholic acid (GDCAS) were differently expressed, what’s more,
all of these 6 BAs were significantly upregulated in the sera of patients with CRC compared with healthy individuals.
Notably, the concentration of GCA was mostly upregulated compared with the other five types of BAs in patients
with CRC (Fig. 1A). It was also found that the levels of GCA in patients with CRC with stage III/IV or distal metastasis
were higher than those found in patients with CRC with stage I/II or without metastasis (Fig. 1B and C). In addition,
increased levels of GCA were positively associated with poor 5-year disease-free and overall survival (Fig. 1D and
E). Univariate and multivariate survival analyses further indicated that serum GCA served as an independent
prognostic biomarker for poor outcome in patients with CRC (Fig. S1A and B). Furthermore, we validated our results
by using an additional CRAC cohort, and confirmed that the serum concentration of GCA was increased in patients
with stage III/IV or distal metastasis (Fig. S1C and D), leading to worse disease-free and overall survival (Fig. S1E
and F). In addition, higher serum GCA concentrations remained significantly associated with both shorter disease-
free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) in CRC patients without liver metastasis (Fig. S1G and H). Take together,
these results indicated that upregulated serum GCA in CRC patients was associated with poor prognosis.

GCA promotes tumor growth in a mouse model of CRC via inhibiting FXR activity. As BAs mainly function by
regulating FXR signaling in the intestine,17, 19 we then examined the effects of FXR with its agonist GW4064 on the
CRC cell lines MC38, CT26, HCT116 and SW620. As expected, activation of FXR by GW4064 significantly
promoted FXR activity (Fig. 1F and S2A). FXR was knocked out in MC38, CT26, HCT116 and SW620 cells with
the CRISPR/Cas9 system (Fig. S2B), and it was found that GW4064 failed to promote FXR activity in Fxr-deficient
mouse and human CRC cells (Fig. S2C). Next, we cultured MC38 cells with 0-200µM of GCA and observed that
GCA suppressed FXR activity in a dose dependent manner (Fig. S2D). Of note, 100nM of GCA robustly decreased
the activation of FXR without affecting the proliferation of MC38 cells, suggesting that this dosage of GCA is optimal
for in vitro experiments (Fig. S2D). Consistently, same tendency was observed in other CRC cells (Fig. 1F and S2A).
And GCA inhibited the transcriptional expression of the FXR downstream genes SHIP and IBABP in these CRC cell
lines confirmed by qPCR (Fig. 1G and S2E). Given that BAs regulate FXR function by altering the expression of FXR
or the ability binding to RXR, which is required for its downstream transcriptional activity23, we performed qPCR as
well as immunoprecipitation experiments, and found that GCA inhibited the interaction between FXR and RXR,
without affecting the mRNA level of FXR itself (Fig. S2F and G). In addition, we also observed that the FXR agonist
was sufficient to restore the expression of SHIP and IBABP in GCA treated MC38 and HCT116 cells (Fig. S2H),
suggesting a negative role of GCA in FXR signaling in CRC.

To further explore the roles of GCA in CRC, MC38, CT26, HCT116 and SW620 cells were incubated with GCA or
GW4064, and it was observed that the treatment had little effect on tumor cell proliferation in vitro (Fig. S2I).
Consistently, the proliferation rate was also comparable in both FXR-deleted (FXR-KO) and control CRC cells (Fig.
S2J). However, by using intestinal epithelial-specific Fxr-knockout (Fxr-ko, Fxr-/-) mice, it was found that Fxr was
successfully deleted in intestine tissues and AOM/DSS-induced tumors (Fig. S2K-L). Loss of FXR promoted the
development of CRC, as evidence by a decreased the colorectal length in the Fxr-ko mice, (Fig. 1H). Histological
analysis showed that tumors derived from Fxr-ko mice exhibited enlarged size and poor differentiation (Fig. 1I). We
also generated another orthotopic mice model of CRC by implanting Fxr-knockout and control MC38 cells into colon
mucosa. Consistently, mice with Fxr-knockout tumors showed an increased tumor growth and a worse overall survival
compared to that of control tumors (Fig. S3A), suggesting that FXR acted as a tumor suppressor in CRC tumorigenesis
in vivo. To further confirm this result, we inoculated MC38 cells into C57BL/6 mice and observed that 400 mg/kg of
GCA treatment (intragastric gavage; ig) robustly increased tumor burden without evident side effects as measured by
weight loss during the cause (Fig. S3B). We next measured the concentrations of BAs significantly elevated in the
serum of CRC patients in mice following GCA administration (400 mg/kg). While serum and tumoral GCA levels
were barely detectable in tumor-bearing mice without GCA treatment, GCA-treated mice exhibited measurable
accumulation, with serum levels reaching approximately 150 nM and tumoral concentrations around 82 nmol/g (Fig.
S3C-D). Notably, the median serum GCA concentrations in human Cohorts I and II were approximately 96.4 nM and
96.7 nM, respectively. These values are comparable to, or slightly lower than, those observed in GCA-treated mice,
supporting the physiological relevance of our experimental model.

Of note, GCA significantly increased the tumor growth in AOM/DSS-induced CRC models, as evidenced by an
increased tumor numbers and a short colon length in mice treated with GCA (Fig. S3E). However, GCA-treatment
could not further promote the tumorigenesis in Fxr-ko C57BL/6 mice, suggesting that FXR is the functional target of
GCA-induced tumorigenesis. While GCA significantly promoted tumor growth and decreased overall survival in
immunocompetent mice by subcutaneously inoculating MC38 or CT26 cells (Fig. S3F and G), no significant
difference was observed in terms of tumor size or survival rate between the GCA-treated and control groups when
MC38 or CT26 cells were inoculated in immunodeficient BALB/c nude mice (Fig. S3H and I). qRT-PCR showed that
GCA suppressed FXR signaling pathway in vivo, as shown by decreased expression of SHIP and IBABP in MC38 or
CT26 tumors derived from immune-competent or nude mice treated with GCA (Fig. S3J and K). To avoid the potential
effects of bacterial transformation of GCA in intestine, we intraperitoneal injected (i.p.ed) GCA twice a week in MC38
tumor-bearing mice and found an increased tumor growth in mice with GCA treatment (Fig. S3L). Collectively, our
data indicated that immune responses played an important role in the GCA-induced development of CRC.

Based on the ability of GCA to inhibit FXR-activity, the present study next investigated whether altering the function
of FXR could affect GCA-mediated tumor growth. Indeed, increased tumor size and decreased survival rate were
observed in immunocompetent mice, but not in BALB/c nude mice, when treating the animals with the FXR antagonist
T-βMCA (Fig. 1J and S4A-B), which mimics the behavior of tumor inoculated in immunocompetent mice or in
immunodeficient mice treated with GCA. Consistently, the suppressive role of FXR in cancer was confirmed when
immunocompetent, but not immunodeficient, BALB/c nude mice were treated with the FXR agonist GW4064 (Fig.
S4C-G). To explore whether impaired FXR signaling was critical for GCA-increased tumor growth in vivo, the mice
were treated with GCA in the absence or presence of the FXR-agonist GW4064 after inoculating MC38 or CT26 cells.
As expected, mice receiving GW4064 showed decreased tumor size and prolonged overall survival compared with
mice treated with GCA alone (Fig. 1K and S4H). Of note, GW4064 reverted the expression of FXR target genes I-
BABP and SHP that inhibited by GCA (S4I and J). Taken together, these data suggested that impairment of FXR-
mediated tumor suppression was critical for GCA-induced tumorigenesis, and immune responses were involved in
regulating the GCA-FXR axis mediated tumor development.

GCA treatment inhibits CD8+ T cell infiltration and antitumor response. To further investigate the effects of
tumor-infiltrated immune cells on GCA/FXR-mediated tumor progression, five independent cell clusters of CD45+
immune cells, including B cells, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, macrophages and natural killer cells, were identified based
on scRNA-seq (Fig. 2A right). An increased total number of CD8+ T cells and macrophages was observed in tumors
treated with GW4064 compared with those without treatment (Fig. 2A left). The expression of markers of immune
subtypes was shown by using a panel of 21 markers (Fig. S5A). Next, MC38 tumors were isolated from mice receiving
GCA (i.g.) for 10 days, and the percentages of subpopulations in immune cells were analyzed by flow cytometry.
Consistently, CD8+ T cells and macrophages, but not CD4+ T cells or CD4+ Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Treg), were
downregulated in tumors treated with GCA (Fig. 2B). To explore whether the suppressive effect of FXR on tumors
was dependent on CD8+ T cells or macrophages, CD8+ T cells or macrophages were depleted in mice by using an their
specific anti-CD8α antibody or clodronate liposomes (Fig. S5B), respectively, before inoculating the mice with MC38
cells with or without GCA or GW4064 treatment. Notably, GCA treatment did not further increase tumor growth in
CD8+ T cell-depleted mice compared with untreated controls (Fig. 2C). Moreover, it was also found that the FXR
agonist failed to inhibit CRC tumor progression in CD8+ T cell-depleted mice (Fig. 2D). However, tumor growth was
comparable in both macrophage-depleted and control mice regardless of GCA or GW4064 treatment (Fig. 2E and F).
In addition, MC38 or CT26 CRC cells were inoculated into Rag1-/- mice (which are deficient in T and B cells), and it
was observed that treatment with FXR antagonist or agonist had a limited effect on tumor growth in Rag1-/- mice (Fig.
S5 C and D). These data suggested that CD8+ T cells, but not macrophages, in the TME were involved in GCA/FXR-
mediated tumor growth.

We next explore the signaling pathway enriched in GCA-induced tumorigenesis, single-cell RNA sequencing analysis
revealed that genes upregulated in FXR signaling-mediated activated tumors were mainly associated with immune
responses, including type I/II IFN responses (Fig. S6A and B). We examined the expression of IFN-stimulated genes
(ISGs), including CXCL9, CXCL10, BST2, STAT1 and IFITM3, by qPCR. As expected, the mRNA levels of these
ISGs were significantly upregulated in MC38 and CT26 tumor tissues derived from immunocompetent mice treated
with GW4064 (Fig. S6C), whereas the expression of ISGs were decreased in tumors treated with GCA (Fig. S6D).
However, the alteration of the mRNA levels of ISGs was not observed in tumor tissues derived from immunodeficient
BALB/c nude mice when treating with GW4064 or GCA (Fig. S6E and F). Interestingly, MC38 and HCT116 cells
were also treated with GW4064 or GCA in culture, however, no significant increase in the transcriptional expression
of these ISGs was observed in GW4064- or GCA-treated CRC cells (Fig. S6G and H), suggesting a dependency on
IFN signaling associated immune responses in vivo.

As IFNγ is critical for tumor suppression mediated by CD8+ tumor-infiltrated T cells, we further used FACS analysis
to evaluate IFNγ-expressing CD8+ T cells. It was found that IFNγ-expressing CD8+ T cells were significantly
decreased in GCA-treated MC38 or CT26 tumors (Fig. 2G, S6I). However, an increased frequency of exhausted PD-
1+ TIM3+ CD8+ T cells was observed in tumors treated with GCA compared with controls (Fig. 2G and S6I). On the
contrary, tumors treated with FXR agonist GW4064 showed an enhanced population of CD8+ IFNγ+ T cells,
accompanied with attenuated exhausted CD8+ T cell infiltration (Fig. 2H and S6J). Thus, the present results suggested
that GCA-induced FXR impaired the antitumor activity of CD8+ T cells in the TME.

Increased expression of PD-L1 is required for GCA-mediated tumorigenesis. To investigate the underlying
molecular mechanisms of GCA-mediated suppression of T cell immune responses, data-independent acquisition MS-
based proteomics was performed in MC38 cells treated with or without GCA. Heatmap showed that PD-L1 was the
most significantly increased protein among the top 20 deferentially expressed proteins (FC≥2, p≤0.05) annotated to
both cytokine production and regulation of immune response pathways in GCA-treated MC38 cells (Fig.2I). Next,
CRC cells were treated with GCA or GW4064 in vitro, and the changes in the mRNA and protein levels of PD-L1
were evaluated. It was found that the levels of protein and cell surface expression of PD-L1, but not its mRNA levels,
were upregulated in tumor cells treated with GCA (Fig. 2J and S7A, C). By contrast, PD-L1 protein levels were
decreased in MC38 cells treated with the FXR agonist GW4064 compared with untreated cells (Fig. 2J, S7B and C),
which suggests that the GCA/FXR-mediated increase in PD-L1 was regulated in a post-transcriptional manner.
Functionally, tumor infiltrated CD8+ T cells were co-cultured with MC38 cells or CT26 cells that had been pre-
pretreated with GCA under anti-CD3 and anti-CD28-stimulating conditions, and it was found that FXR-inactivation
rendered CRC cells more resistant to CD8+ T cells in T cell-mediated tumor cell-killing assays (Fig. S7D). Furthermore,
tumor cell killing capacity was increased in wild-type (WT), but not in Cd274-KO, CRC cells pre-treated with a FXR
agonist (Fig. S7E). We further corroborated the results with in vivo subcutaneous tumor growth model and found that
knockout of Cd274 in MC38 cells or CT26 cells significantly reverted GCA-induced tumorigenesis (Fig. 2K and L).
qRT-PCR analysis revealed that CD274-knockout did not affect GCA-induced suppression of FXR downstream genes
I-BAPA and SHP (Fig. S7F and G). While low-dose anti-PD-L1 (10mg/kg) therapy have minimal effect on tumor
suppression in GCA-treated mice with subcutaneous tumors or in Fxr-/- mice of AOM/DSS-induced CRC model,
blockade of PD-L1/PD-1-signaling with a high-dose of anti-PD-L1 (100 mg/kg) effectively reversed GCA-induced
tumorigenesis (Fig. S7H-J), suggesting that increased PD-L1 expression in tumors is critical for GCA/FXR-mediated
dysfunction of CD8+ T cells during tumor growth.

GCA accelerates PD-L1 palmitoylation via DHHC9 in tumor cells. Since GCA treatment did not alter the
transcriptional levels of PD-L1 in CRC cells, we next suppressed the common degradation pathways that are involved
in the regulation of PD-L1. It was observed that GCA-mediated total and surface PD-L1 accumulation was reversed
by 2-bromopalmitate, a general palmitoylation inhibitor, not by the autophagy inhibitor 3-MA or the proteasome
inhibitor MG-132 in CRC cells (Fig. 3A and B). Similarly, increased expression of PD-L1 was observed in CRC cells
treated with palmostatin B, the inhibitor of acyl protein thioesterase 1, which promotes global palmitoylation, in a
dose-dependent manner (Fig. 3C). Moreover, GCA enhanced the palmitoylation modification of PD-L1 in CRC cells
according to the results of Click-iT labelling assay, indicating that GCA stabilized the PD-L1 protein via
palmitoylation (Fig. 3D).

To explore the key palmitoyltransferases for GCA-mediated PD-L1 accumulation, the transcriptional levels of
palmitoyltransferases were screened by RNA-sequencing analysis, and it was found that the expression levels of
DHHC9, DHHC1, DHHC1A2, DHHC18 and DHHC24 were on the top rank of differentially expressed genes in GCA-
treated cells compared with controls (Fig. 3E). Then we knocked down these candidates in MC38 and HCT116 CRC
cells by using specific siRNAs and found that GCA-induced accumulation of the total and cell surface PD-L1 protein
was significantly reduced in DHHC9-knockdown CRC cells but not in other palmitoyltransferases-knockdown CRC
cells (Fig. 3F and G). In addition, the transcriptional levels of DHHC9 were significantly upregulated in GCA-treated
CRC cells confirmed by qPCR (Fig. S8A). To further investigate the function of DHHC9 in regulating the
palmitoylation modification on PD-L1, DHHC9 was overexpressed in CRC cells. Increased protein, but not mRNA,
expression of PD-L1 was observed in DHHC9-ovexpressing CRC cells (Fig. 3H and S8B). Notably, the palmitoylation
modification on PD-L1 was significantly accumulated with the overexpression of DHHC9 (Fig. 3I). Next, we
evaluated whether DHHC9 was critical for GCA-mediated PD-L1 expression. As expected, a decreased protein
expression, but not transcriptional expression, of PD-L1 was observed in DHHC9-knockdown cells treated with GCA
(Fig. S8C and D). Functionally, it was found that the tumor cell killing capacity of tumor-derived CD8+ T cells was
significantly increased when co-cultured with DHHC9-knockdown CRC cells even without treatment with GCA (Fig.
3J). By contrast, overexpressing DHHC9 in MC38 or CT26 cells decreased the killing capacity of CD8+ T cells,
leading to increased tumor growth (Fig. 3K). Furthermore, this tumor promoting capacity could not be reversed by
treatment with the FXR agonist GW4064 (Fig. 3K). Collectively, these results indicated that DHHC9-mediated
palmitoylation modification was critical for the GCA/FXR-induced stabilization of PD-L1 and tumor growth.

The SOX14-DHHC9 axis regulates PD-L1 expression in CRC cells. To identify the TF(s) which is (are) responsible
for the GCA-mediated regulation of tumor PD-L1 expression, we analyzed all the differentially expressed
transcriptional factors with fold change (FC) ≥ 2 in CRC cells treated with GCA, and it was observed that SOX14 was
on the top list of the candidate TFs in terms of FC in expression (Fig. 4A). Loss-of-function screenings were then
performed using specific siRNAs target to top 5 candidate TFs. The results showed that knockdown of SOX14, but
not other candidates, could significantly diminish the expression of PD-L1 protein in CRC cells (Fig. 4B). Moreover,
the mRNA expression of FXR downstream gene IBABP was negatively associated with SOX14 expression in tumor
tissues derived from 80 patients with CRC (Fig. 4C upper). Subsequently, we explored whether FXR directly inhibited
SOX14 transcription. The promoter region of human SOX14 was screened for FXR-binding site by using the JASPAR
database, and ChIP assay was performed with an anti-FXR antibody under GCA or GW4064 treatment conditions. It
was observed that FXR directly bound to the promoter of SOX14 (site 2), as evidenced by the enrichment of the target
sequence (Fig. S9A). Moreover, GCA inhibited the DNA-binding capacity of FXR, whereas the FXR agonist GW4064
promoted its binding with DNA in CRC cells. (Fig. S9B). Finally, luciferase reporter constructs were generated to test
the transcriptional activity of WT and FXR-binding sequence deficiency mutated regions for FXR-binding sites (site
2). As expected, the luciferase activity was significantly increased in HCT116 and SW620 cells transfected with WT
region constructs upon GCA stimulation (Fig. S9C). By contrast, GW4064 significantly decreased the luciferase
activity of CRC cells with WT region constructs, but not of cells transfected with mut region constructs (Fig. S6C),
suggesting that FXR acts as a transcriptional suppressor for SOX14 expression. It was also found that knockdown of
SOX14 decreased PD-L1 expression by using shRNA targeting SOX14 in multiple CRC cell lines even though treated
with GCA (Fig. 4D left, E, and S9D-F). Of note, increased protein levels of PD-L1 were observed in SOX14-
overexpressing cells (Fig. 4F left and G, and S9E), suggesting that increased SOX14 expression may be involved in
GCA-induced PD-L1 expression. Moreover, we also investigated whether SOX14 was involved in regulating GCA-
mediated tumor promoting function by inoculating SOX14-knockdown cells into the subcutaneous tissue or colon
mucosa of mice treated with GCA. Then, we found that Sox14 deficiency inhibited GCA-induced tumor growth,
which was accompanied by an increased frequency of tumor-infiltrating total CD8+ T cells, as well as CD8+ IFNγ+ T
cell subset, but a decreased number of exhausted CD8+ T cells in both subcutaneous and orthotopic CRC model (Fig.
4H and I, S9G and H). The data indicated that SOX14 was a key TF in regulating GCA-mediated PD-L1 expression.

To identify whether SOX14 directly regulates DHHC9 expression, we firstly analyzed the correlation between the
mRNA expression of SOX14 and DHHC9 in 80 human CRC samples, and found that SOX14 was positively correlated
with DHHC9 mRNA expression (Fig. 4C down). It was also validated that GCA significantly increased the
transcription and protein expression of SOX14 and DHHC9, as well as PD-L1 protein expression, in murine MC38
and human HCT116 cells (Fig. 4D right and E). However, knockdown of SOX14 decreased the transcriptional
expression of DHHC9, as well as the protein levels of both DHHC9 and PD-L1 in CRC cells when treated with GCA
(Fig. 4D right and E). By contrast, increased DHHC9 and PD-L1 expressions were observed in CRC cells with SOX14
overexpression compared with control cells (Fig. 4F right and G). Most importantly, FXR-mediated DHHC9 and PD-
L1 inhibition could be reversed by overexpression of SOX14 in cells incubated with a FXR agonist (Fig. 4F right and
G), suggesting that SOX14 is a potent FXR downstream TF for inducing DHHC9 transcriptional expression. Next,
we analyzed the JASPAR database and identified two SOX14-binding sequences on the promoter region of human
DHHC9 by ChIP assay. Only the predicted site 1binding sequence was enriched in ChIP-enriched promoters (Fig. 4J
and K). Moreover, luciferase reporter constructs with SOX14-binding deficiency mutated regions for SOX14-binding
were generated to evaluate transcriptional activity, and found that luciferase activity was significantly increased in
SOX14-overexpressing MC38 and HCT116 cells transfected with DHHC9 WT region constructs, but not in cells
transfected with DHHC9mut region constructs (Fig. 4L). This indicated that SOX14 was critical for DHHC9
expression.

Next, we examined whether DHHC9 was involved in SOX14-mediated tumor progression by overexpressing DHHC9
in SOX14-knockdown CRC cells. We found that overexpression of DHHC9 increased the expression of PD-L1 in
CRC cells that exhibited downregulated PD-L1 expression by SOX14-knockdown (Fig. S9I). And overexpression of
DHHC9 blocked SOX14 deficiency-mediated tumor inhibition (Fig. S9I). In addition, overexpression of DHHC9 in
SOX14-deficient cells led to increased infiltration of total CD8+ T and CD8+ IFNγ+ T effector cells, but decreased
infiltration of exhausted PD-1+ TIM3+ CD8+ T cells (Fig. S9J). Taken together, these data revealed that DHHC9 was
the transcriptional and functional target of SOX14.

The GCA-mediated SOX14/DHHC9 axis correlates with decreased efficacy of immunotherapy in CRC patients.
To further understand the role of the GCA-regulated SOX14/DHHC9 axis in immunotherapy in patients with CRC,
LC-MS analysis was performed in the serum of 41 patients with MSI-H mCRC who received PD-1 blockade alone or
combination with chemotherapy. The majority of patients with mCRC (15/20) with high levels of GCA were predicted
non-responsive for immunotherapy, while patients with mCRC (19/21) with low concentrations of GCA showed
response to immunotherapy (Table S2). Magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography showed that patient
27 had a relatively high level of serum GCA and tumor progression after PD-1 blockade treatment (Fig. 5A, left and
C), whereas patient 14, with a low concentration of serum GCA, showed tumor regression (Fig. 5A, right and C).
We also examined SOX14 and DHHC9 proteins by using IF in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissues from
patients with mCRC who received PD-1 blockade. The majority of mCRC patients with high concentrations of serum
GCA showed strong SOX14, DHHC9 and PD-L1 staining accompanied by low number of CD8+ T cells and often
insensitivity to anti-PD-1 therapy (Fig. 5B and C). On the contrary, patients with low levels of serum GCA exhibited
opposite results (Fig. 5B and C). Furthermore, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis revealed a significant correlation
between the high levels of GCA, SOX14, DHHC9 and PD-L1 and shorter progression-free survival (PFS) rates of
patients with mCRC who received anti-PD-1 therapy (Fig. 5D-G). Conversely, higher number of infiltrated intratumor
CD8+ T cells were accompanied by prolonged PFS rates in patients with CRC who received anti PD-1 therapy (Fig.
5H). Spearman correlation analysis showed that SOX14 protein expression was positively correlated with DHHC9
and PD-L1 protein expression in CRC tumor samples according to the IF staining scores (Fig. 5I and J). DHHC9
protein expression was also positively associated with PD-L1 protein (Fig.5K). We further confirmed our results that
the serum level of GCA was associated with the expression of DHHC9 or SOX14 in tumors of CRC patients in another
cohort (Fig.S10 A-B). Additionally, DHHC9 staining was correlated with SOX14 staining in these CRC tumors
(Fig.S10C). Altogether, these results suggested that GCA regulated SOX14/DHHC9/PD-L1 axis played significant
role on the efficacy of immunotherapy in mCRC, which may be useful as potential prognostic markers for PD-1
blockade in future.

Inhibition of GCA/FXR-induced SOX14 and DHHC9 expression sensitizes CRC to anti-PD-1 therapy. To
explore whether the SOX14-DHHC9-PD-L1 axis is critical for GCA/FXR-mediated immunosuppression, it was
hypothesized that Sox14-knockdown (Sox-KD) could ameliorate anti-PD-1 treatment in CRC under high levels of
GCA in the TME. Then, GCA-treated immunocompetent mice were engrafted with control or Sox14-KD CRC cells
and found that knockdown of Sox14 inhibited MC38 colon cancer outgrowth in the presence of anti-PD-1 therapy
(Fig. 6A). Moreover, increased infiltration of CD8+ T and CD8+ IFNγ+ T effector cells, while decreased exhausted
CD8+ T cells were observed in Sox14-KD cells compared with control cells in mice with and without anti-PD-1
antibody (Fig. 6B). Consistently, knockdown of Dhhc9 also significantly suppressed tumor growth in mice subjected
to anti-PD-1 therapy compared with mice with monotreatment. In addition, Dhhc9-deficiency enhanced the CD8+ T
cell anti-tumor function in the TME, as evidenced by the proportion of CD8+ T and IFNγ+ CD8+ T enriched in Dhhc9-
knockdown MC38 tumors with anti-PD-1 treatment (Fig. 6C and D). As GCA negatively regulated FXR activity, we
further investigated whether a FXR agonist could synergize CRC cells to anti-PD-1 therapy. As expected, combined
GW4064 and anti-PD-1 treatment robustly slowed the tumor growth, which as associated with a higher number of
CD8+ IFNγ+ T effector cell infiltration and lower percentage of exhausted T cells in tumors compared with those
receiving monotherapies, suggesting that the activation of FXR sufficiently promoted the antitumor effects of anti-
PD-1 therapy (Fig. S11A-D). In addition, anti-PD-1 therapy slightly decreased the AOM/DSS-mediated CRC
tumorigenesis in both C57ABL/6 and BALB/c mice (Fig. S11E-F). Of note, we observed that mice treated with
combined anti-PD-1 and GW4064 were most likely to benefit from therapy, as evidenced by an increased colon length
with a decreased tumor numbers and areas in mice receiving combined treatment compared to mono-treatment (Fig.
S11E and F). To strengthen the present conclusions, anti-PD-1-resistant MC38 (MC38R) colon cancer was generated
by three rounds of in vivo/in vitro selection. Anti-PD-1 antibody had a limited effect on the growth of MC38R cells
in both subcutaneous and orthotopic CRC models (Fig. 6E and F, S11G and H). However, GW4064 inhibited MC38R
tumor growth and sensitized MC38R cells to anti-PD-1 therapy, which was accompanied by a significantly increased
antitumor response of CD8+ T cells, as evidenced by increased infiltration of CD8+ T and CD8+ IFNγ+ T effector cells,
and decreased exhausted CD8+ T cells in tumors compared with GW4064 monotreatment (Fig. 6E and F, S11G and
H). The data indicated that combining FXR agonist with anti-PD-1 therapy enhanced the efficacy of anti-PD-1 in
resistant colon cancer.
