## Methods

Patient biopsies. A total of 80 paired CRC tissues, adjacent normal mucosa tissues and serum collected between
January 2018 and September 2018 from patients with CRC who were diagnosed at Fudan University Shanghai Cancer
Center (FUSCC) were used for measuring the concentrations of a series of BAs and for tissue immunofluorescence
staining (cohort Ⅰ). In addition, the serum of 20 normal healthy individuals was collected in October 2018. Furthermore,
41 patients with MSI-H or dMMR with recurrence or distant metastasis who received anti PD-1 immunotherapy
between February 2019 and September 2021 at FUSCC were enrolled in the present study (cohort Ⅱ). A cohort of 308
patients (Cohort III) with colorectal cancer (CRC) was enrolled between January 2008 and September 2009 at Fudan
University Shanghai Cancer Center. Their clinicopathological characteristics of the patients are summarized in
Supplementary Data 1-3. All patients from these 3 cohorts did not receive any treatment for cancer before surgery.
Human serum specimens were collected prior to tumor resection, while normal mucosa and paired cancer tissues, as
well as metastatic tissues, were collected immediately after surgical resection. Written informed consent was obtained
from each patient, and the study protocol both conformed to the ethical guidelines of the 1975 Declaration of Helsinki
and was approved by the Ethics Committee of FUSCC (approval no. 050432-4-2108).

Cell lines, plasmids, lentivirus production and transduction. The HCT116 and SW620 human colon cancer cell
lines, the CT26 mouse colon cancer cell line, and the 293T cell line were obtained from the American Type Culture
Collection, while the MC38 mouse colon cancer cell line was purchased from the Cell Bank of the Institute of
Biochemistry and Cell Biology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Cell lines were cultured at 37˚C in 5% CO2 in
DMEM or in RPMI1640 supplemented with 10% fetal calf serum, 100 U/ml penicillin and 100 µg/ml streptomycin.
Cells were tested monthly and found to be free of mycoplasm by PCR-based screening. Full-length SOX14 and
DHHC9 fused with Flag-tag were amplified via PCR from cDNA of HCT116 cells, and then recombined into the
pLVX plasmid (cat. no. 125839; Addgene, Inc.). The primers used are listed in Supplementary Data 4. Short hairpin
RNA (shRNA) sequences targeting SOX14 and DHHC9 were cloned into the pLKO.1 vector (cat. no. 10878; Addgene,
Inc.), and the primers used are listed in Supplementary Data 5. Single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting FXR or CD274
were constructed into the lentiCRISPR v2 vector (cat. no. 52961; Addgene, Inc.). CRISPR/Cas9 targeting sequences
are listed in Supplementary Data 5. Lentivirus was produced by transiently transfecting 293T cells with
Lipofectamine® 3000 transfection reagent (cat. no. L3000075; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) according to the
manufacturer’s instructions. The viral supernatants were then incubated with 8 μg/ml Polybrene for 24 h, and the viral
supernatants were then exchanged for fresh media. Cells were incubated for 48 h before puromycin selection. For
small interfering RNA (siRNA) transfection, tumor cells were seeded into 6-well plates at ~1.5x105 cells per well and
incubated at 37˚C overnight. Specific siRNAs (5 nM; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) were transfected into cells and
incubated for 6 h. Next, the medium was replaced with complete DMEM for 48 h. The siRNA sequences are listed in
Supplementary Data 6. The anti-PD1-resistant MC38R tumor cells were developed as previously described.37 In brief,
6-week-old C57BL/6J mice were injected subcutaneously into the right flank with 1.0x106 MC38 cells (n=6). At 10
days post-injection, mice were treated twice weekly with 100 μg anti-PD-1α antibody (Bio X Cell) per mouse via
intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection for 1 week. Next, tumors were selected and transplanted into the right flank of 6-week-
old C57BL/6J mice. After 3 repeated cycles of tumor selection, nonresponsive tumors were digested into single tumor
cells, namely MC38R tumor cells.

Sample preparation and HPLC-MS/MS-based metabolomic approaches.
100 μl serum were spiked with 0.51 ml of ice-cold MeOH-ACN (1:1, v:v). The sample was vortexed and incubated
for 1h at - 20 °C, following by centrifuging at 14000 rcf at 4 °C for 15 min to precipitate proteins. The supernatant
was aspirated, evaporated using a vacuum concentrator (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The extracts were
reconstituted in 100 μl of MeOH and deionized water (85:15, v:v), and centrifuged at at 15000 g at 4 °C for 15 min to
remove insoluble debris. The supernatant was collected at UPLC autosampler vials (Thermo Scientific, MA, USA)
and stored at - 80 °C prior to UPLC-MS analysis. Tumor samples were homogenized in 100% acetonitrile and were
centrifuged twice at 15,000g for 30 minutes at 4°C for removal of precipitated proteins and other particulates to remove
precipitated proteins and particulates. The supernatant was then diluted with 0.1% formic acid. The quality control
sample was pooled by mixing 5 μL of extracted solution from each sample.

Liquid chromatographic separation and mass spectrometric detection were conducted using the Thermo Scientific
TSQ Quantum Ultra LC-MS/MS system (Thermo Fisher, Palo Alto, CA). Chromatographic separation was achieved
on a Poroshell SB-C18 analytical column (particle size, 1.7 μm; 50 mm (length) × 2.1 mm (i.d.)) equipped with a BEH
C18 VanGuard pre-column (5 × 2.1 mm, i.d.; 1.7 μm). The mobile phase consisted of aqueous buffer containing 1 mM
ammonium formate and formic acid (pH 4.39) (A) and acetonitrile/isopropanol (1:1 v/v) (B), with a total flow rate of
0.4 ml/min. The gradient profile for the LC pumps was as follows: 20–30% B (0-3 min), 30-40% B (3-4 min), 50-70%
B (4-5 min), 70-90% B (5-5.2 min), continuing at 90% B up to 6 min. The injection volume for all samples was 2 μl.
The column temperature was set to 55 °C, and the sample tray temperature was maintained at 8 °C. For mass
spectrometric detection, the electrospray ionization (ESI) source was operated in negative ion mode to produce
MS/MS spectra (Thermo Fisher). The parameters were as follows: spray voltage 2 kV, cone voltage 30 V, source
temperature 120 °C, desolvation temperature 500 °C, cone gas flow 50 L/h, desolations gas flow 900 L/h.

For preparation of standard stock, 33 bile acid were dissolved to 1 mg/mL by appropriate amount of methanol as
standard stock solutions and then further diluted to obtain standard solutions containing 0.05, 0.5, 5, and 50 mg/mL
of each bile acid. The supernatant was collected and 70 μl was injected into the LC–MS/MS system for analysis.
Cholic acid (CA), chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA), sodium glycochenodeoxycholate (GCDCA), sodium
taurochenodeoxycholate (TCDCA), glycocholic acid (GCA), taurolithocholic acid (TLCA), sodium
taurodeoxycholate hydrate (TDCA), and taurocholic acid sodium salt hydrate (TCA) was purchased from Sigma-
Aldrich (Saint Louis, MO). Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), deoxycholic acid (DCA). Lithocholic acid (LCA) and
glycoursodeoxycholic acid (GUDCA) were procured from Cayman Chemical Company (Ann Arbor, MI, USA).
Glycodeoxycholic acid (GDCA) and glycolithocholic acid (GLCA) were acquired from Toronto Research Chemicals
(TRC, Canada).

Data‐independent acquisition mass spectrometry (MS)‐based proteomics. MC38 cells were treated with or
without GCA for 24 h and processed by Data Independent Acquisition6 individually to assess the proteome. In brief,
for sample preparation, cells were lysed in lysis buffer (1% SDS and 8 M urea) and digested with iST Sample
Preparation kit (PreOmics) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Peptides were eluted with elution buffer (2 x
100 µl) and then lyophilized by SpeedVac. Protein samples were reconstituted in 0.1% FA and subjected to UltiMate
3000 liquid chromatography (LC) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.). In total, 200 ng peptide was separated by an
analytical column with a 60 min gradient starting at 4% buffer B (80% ACN with 0.1% FA), followed by a stepwise
increase to 28% in 25 min, 44% in 10 min, 90% in 10 min, hold for 7 min, and then equilibration at 4% for 8 min. The
column flow rate was maintained at 500 nl/min with a column temperature of 50˚C. DIA data were acquired in the
diaPASEF mode. Raw data of DIA were analyzed by Spectronaut 17 (Biognosys AG) with default settings. The
normalization strategy was set to local normalization. Peptides which passed the 1% Q-value cut-off were used to
calculate the major group quantities with the MaxLFQ method. Differentially expressed proteins were selected based
on P<0.05, fold-change (FC)>1.5 or FC<1/1.5.

Dual Luciferase Reporter Assay. For measurement of FXR activity, cells were seeded into 24-well plates at ~1.5x104
cells per well and transfected with the FXR luciferase reporter plasmid FXRE-Luc (200 ng; cat. no. 11764ES03;
Shanghai Yeasen Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) and 20 ng Renilla pRL-SV40P plasmid (cat. no. 27163; Addgene, Inc.) per
well with Lipofectamine® 3000 according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Next, cells were treated with GCA
(100nM, cat. no. G2878; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck KGaA) or GW4064 (5μM, cat. no. G5172; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck
KGaA) for 24 h, and the relative luciferase units (RLUs) were measured using the Dual-Glo Luciferase Assay System
(Promega Corporation) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For monitoring SOX9 or DHHC9 expression,
cells were seeded and transfected with 200 ng pGL3-SOX14, pGL3-SOX14-FXR mutant 15, pGL3-DHHC9 or pGL3-
DHHC9-SOX14 mut vector, along with 20 ng Renilla pRL-SV40P plasmid per well with Lipofectamine® 2000. After
24 h, the RLUs in cells were measured using the Dual-Glo Luciferase Assay System. The firefly RLUs were
normalized by the RLUs from the Renilla-containing vector.

Mice. Fxr floxed mice were purchased from Cyagen Biosciences, Inc. (cat. no. S-CKO-04890). Villin-Cre (#004586)
transgenic mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME, USA) to create conditional knockout
mice and silenced the expression of Fxr in intestinal epithelial cells. Briefly, two synthesized sgRNAs targeting introns
3 and 4, Cas9 mRNA and LoxP-containing oligonucleotide flanking with 50-bp homology arms were injected into
mouse zygotes and then transferred into pseudo-pregnant mice. Fxr floxed mice were identified by genotyping and
sequencing. Fxr floxed mice were then crossed with villin-Cre transgenic mice to obtain intestinal epithelial-specific
Fxr knockout mouse models. The mice were randomly assigned into experimental groups. For primary mouse models,
animals were chosen based on correct genotypes and were co-allocated in the same cages and used for the studies. All
mice used in the study were gender- and age-matched. Investigators were blinded to the treatments during the
experiments. All mice were housed in the specific-pathogen free animal facility of FUSCC. Animals were observed
for general health and signs of distress (reduced weight, ruffled fur, or evidence of tumor ulceration/bleeding). Mice
were euthanized when body weight loss exceeded 20% or when tumor volume exceeded 1,500 mm³. Euthanasia was
performed in accordance with institutional and guidelines by CO₂ inhalation followed by cervical dislocation to ensure
death. The maximal tumor burden permitted by our ethics committee is 1,500 mm³, and this limit was not exceeded
in any experiment. All animal procedures were approved by the Animal care and Use Committee of FUSCC.
For tumor engraftment, 6-week-old C57BL/6J or BALB/c mice were injected subcutaneously into the right flank with
1.0x106 MC38 or CT26 cells, respectively. BALB/c nude mice were also used to establish a subcutaneous CRC model
by using MC38 or CT26 cells. The tumor volumes were calculated by using the formula ‘length x width x width/2’ at
the indicated days. Body weight was recorded at the time of tumor measurement. For survival analysis, mice were
considered moribund and euthanized when tumor volume reached approximately 1000 mm³ or when severe signs of
distress were observed. For endoscopy-guided orthotopic mouse model, wild-type 10-12 weeks old C57BL/6 mice
were examined by endoscopy Coloview® system (Storz, Tuttlingen, Germany) with a zero-degree optic (diameter 1.9
mm) to ensure the colonic mucosa was healthy prior to implantation after anesthesia. For tumor cell implantation, the
colon was first washed with PBS at 37 °C and 0.5×106 MC38 cells) diluted in 50 μL of PBS were injected very slowly
towards the lumen of lower mid and distal colon ~30 mm from the anal verge to induce tumor growth by using
endoscopic injection. The tumor volume was endoscopically monitored weekly by endoscopic score. For the
AOM/DSS-induced colitis-associated cancer model, 8 to 10-week-old male mice were injected i.p. with 10 mg/kg
AOM (cat. no. A5486; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck KGaA). After 5 days, 2% DSS (cat. no. D8906; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck
KGaA) was added to the drinking water for 5 days, followed by regular drinking water for 2 weeks. The mice were
sacrificed after 3 repeated cycles of DSS. For the macrophage-depletion experiment, the mice were pretreated with
clodronate liposome (150 μl; Max Scientific) 3 days before inoculating with tumor cells, and then the indicated mice
were administered with clodronate and control liposomes, with or without GCA [400 mµg/kg, intragastric gavage (ig)
or GW4064 (50 mg/kg, i.p.)] twice per week during the course of the experiments. For the CD8-depletion experiment,
mice were treated with an anti-CD8 antibody (200 µg per injection; clone 2.43; Bio X Cell) twice weekly during the
course of the experiments. For anti-PD-1 antibody treatment, mice were treated with 100 μg anti-PD-1α antibody (Bio
X Cell) per mouse twice weekly or the corresponding IgG control via i.p. injection for the indicated days. For anti-
PD-L1 antibody treatment, mice were treated with 10 mg/kg or 100mg/kg anti-PD-L1 antibody (Bio X Cell) per mouse
twice weekly or the corresponding IgG control via i.p. injection for the indicated days. For GCA (400 mg/kg,
intragastric gavage), GW4064 (50 mg/kg, i.p.) or T-βMCA (400 mg/kg, i.p.) treatment, mice were treated with
GW4064 or T-βMCA twice per week after 6 days of being inoculated with the indicated CRC cells.

mRNA extraction and reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Total RNA was extracted from cells
or tumors by using TRizol® reagent (cat. no. 15596026CN; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) according to the
manufacturer’s instructions. Next, the extracted RNA was reversely transcribed to cDNA with PrimeScript® RT
Reagent Kit (cat. no. RR037B; Takara Bio, Inc.). RT-qPCR was conducted with a fast two-step amplification program
using FastStart Universal SYBR Green Master Mix (cat. no. 04913850001; Roche Diagnostics GmbH). Data were
normalized to GAPDH. The primers used are listed in Supplementary Data 7.

Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay. HCT116- and SW620-expressing SOX14-Flag CRC cells, or CRC
cells treated with GCA or GW4064 for 24 h, were subjected to ChIP assay with SimpleChIP® Enzymatic Chromatin
IP Kit (cat. no. 9003S; Cell Signaling Technology, Inc.) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Mouse monoclonal
antibody specific for FXR (cat. no. 72105; Cell Signaling Technology, Inc.) and rabbit monoclonal antibody specific
for SOX14 (cat. no. PA1-28074; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) were used for ChIP assay. SYBR Green RT-qPCR
was performed by using the following primers: FXR binding site 1 forward: 5’-TTTGTATTTCAAGCCCTAA-3’ and
reverse: 5’-GACTTCGGTTCCACATTGT-3’; FXR binding site 2 forward: 5’-CAGTCTAGAGCTAGCCTCT-3’ and
reverse: 5’-CGCACCTGCCAACACGCCGG-3’; SOX14 binding site 1 forward: 5’-
AGGGAGATGGGTGGAGGAGT-3’ and reverse 5’-CGGCCGCCCCTATC-3’; and SOX14 binding site 2 forward:
5’-GGAGGCGCCGAGGCC-3’ and reverse: 5’-CCCACCACTGGCCAAAT-3’.

Immunoblotting. For immunoblotting, samples harvested form cells or tumors were lysed with RIPA buffer (cat. no.
89901; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) supplemented with a protease inhibitor (cat. no.
05892970001; Roche Diagnostics GmbH) and a phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (cat. no. 04906845001;
Roche Diagnostics GmbH) for 1 h. The lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4˚C. The supernatants
were collected, and equal quantities of cell lysates (100 μg) were mixed with 5X SDS-PAGE loading dye. Next, the
samples were separated using 10% SDS-PAGE and transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes (MilliporeSigma). The
membranes were then incubated with the indicated primary and secondary antibodies and visualized using the
SuperSignal West Dura Extended Duration Substrate (cat. no. 34076; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.). The antibodies
employed are listed in Supplementary Data 8.

Immunofluorescence microscopy and multiplex immunofluorescence staining. For immunofluorescence
microscopy assay, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, followed by permeabilization with 0.5%
Triton X-100 for 15 min. Samples were blocked with 1% goat serum for 30 min, and then incubated with the indicated
primary antibodies at 4˚C for 12 h before being incubated at room temperature with secondary antibodies conjugated
to Alexa Fluor 488/594. DAPI (cat. no. ab104139; Abcam) was used to stain the nuclei for 30 min before subjecting
the samples to Zeiss Axiovert-200 fluorescence microscope (Zeiss AG).

For multiplex staining, samples were treated following the Opal protocol staining method. The reagents used were as
follows: Anti-SOX14 (cat. no. #ab214041; 1:500; Abcam), anti-DHHC9, anti-PD-L1 and anti-CD8 (cat. no. 98941;
Cell Signaling Technology, Inc.; RRID: AB_2756376, 1:500) antibodies were visualized by using fluorescein-cyanine
(Cy) 7 (1:50), fluorescein-Cy5 (1:50) and fluorescein-Cy3 (1:50). In addition, DAPI (1:2,000) was used for nuclei
staining. All sections were cover slipped using VECTASHIELD Hardset Antifade Mounting Medium (cat. no. #H-
1400; Vector Laboratories). The slides were scanned, and the mean fluorescence intensity of the indicated markers
was analyzed with a Vectra slide scanner (PerkinElmer, Inc.) under fluorescence conditions.

Co-culture assay. MC38 or CT26 cells were injected (1.0x106 cells) subcutaneously into the right flank of C57BL/6
or BALB/c mice for 2 weeks. Next, the CD8+ T cells in MC38 or CT26 tumors were isolated by FACs. The number
of indicated MC38 cells or CT26 cells was counted after 3 days of co-culture with CD8+ T cells (1.0x104 cells) in the
presence of anti-CD3 (5 μg/ml) and anti-CD28 (5 μg/ml) antibody.

Tumor digestion, cell isolation and flow cytometry analysis. Tumors derived from the indicated mice were sheared
and digested by using digestion buffer [RPMI medium supplemented with 5% FBS, intravenous collagenase I (0.5
mg/mL, cat. no. C1-22; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck KGaA) and DNase (1 µg/ml; cat. no. D5025; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck
KGaA) for 30 min at 37˚C. Next, the mixture was filtered, and red blood cells (RBCs) were lysed using RBC lysis
buffer (cat. no. 00-4300-54; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.). The precipitates were washed with buffer II (PBS with
2% FBS) and blocked with anti-CD16/32 antibody for 30 min. The single-cell suspensions were washed and incubated
with the indicated antibodies before being subjected to LSRII (BPD Biosciences) for analysis. Data were analyzed using
FlowJo. The antibodies used are listed in Table S8. Cell populations were identified based on the following expression
markers: CD4 T cells: CD45+/CD4+; CD8 T cells: CD45+/ CD8+; MDSC cells: CD45+/CD11b+/Gr-1+; and
macrophages: CD45+/CD11b+/F4/80+. For intracellular staining, cells were stimulated with phorbol 12-myristate 13-
acetate (20 ng/ml; cat. no. p8139; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck KGaA), ionomycin (1 μg/ml; cat. no. 13909; Sigma‐Aldrich;
Merck KGaA) and brefeldin A (5 ng/ml; cat. no. B5936; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck KGaA) for 4 h and then stained
according to the intracellular cytokine staining procedure. Gate strategy (Fig.S12) and representative image of tumors
(Fig.S13) were shown in supplementary Figures.

Single cell sorting, library preparation and sequencing and data preprocessing. Tumor single-cell suspensions
were prepared and filtered over 40-µm cell strainers. Next, cell concentration and viability were evaluated by Trypan
Blue staining. The isolated cells were subjected to single cell RNA analysis. In brief, cells were loaded to prepare
single-cell gel beads in emulsions (GEMs) by using Chromium Single Cell Controller Instrument (10x Genomics).
GEMs were encapsulated using the Single Cell 3’ Library & Cell Bead Kit (10x Genomics). Completed libraries were
sequenced by Illumina NovaSeq 6000 using high-output 75-cycle kits with 150-bp paired-end reads. The data files
were analyzed with the R package SingleR. Gene transcript counts per cell and was determined by the unique
molecular identifier (UMI; R package Seurat, version 3.1.1). After removing low-quality cells and likely multiplet
captures, Seurat (normalizeData function) was used to normalize the expression values for each cell by the total
expression and log-transformed the results. FindVariableGenes function in Seurat was performed to identify the highly
variable genes. Then, these genes were subjected to RunPCA function and FindClusters function of Seurat to calculate
the significant principal components. The clusters were visualized in a two-dimensional t-SNE algorithm using the
RunTSNE function in Seurat and the marker genes of each cluster were identified by The FindAllMarkers function in
Seurat. Additionally, differentially expressed genes (DEGs, P< 0.05 and |log2 (fold-change)| >0.58) was filtered by
the FindMarkers function. Then, SingleR, was used for unbiased cell type recognition of scRNA-seq, with the
reference transcriptomic datasets ‘Human Primary Cell Atlas’ to infer the origin of each single cell independently and
to identify cell types.38 Gene Ontology enrichment pathway enrichment analyses of DEGs were carried out using the
hypergeometric distribution of R software. For immune cells, CD45+ cells were gated, and five major clusters of
immune cells were identified, including CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, macrophages, B cells, neutrophils and NK cells
by using markers for inferring immune cell populations in time-of-flight (CyTOF) analysis as previous study39.
Sequencing and bioinformatics analysis were performed by Shanghai OE Biotech Co., Ltd.

PD-L1 palmitoylation. Tumor cells were co-cultured with complete medium containing 100 μM Click-iT Palmitic
Acid-Azide (cat. no. C10265; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) at 37˚C and 5% CO2 for 6 h. Next, the cells were
harvested and lysed with lysis buffer (1% SDS in 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0) supplemented with a protease inhibitor
and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail on ice for 0.5 h. After sonication, the cell lysate was centrifuged at 12,000 x g at
4˚C for 10 min. The supernatants of cell lysates were collected and subject to Click-iT assay by using the Click-iT
Protein Reaction Buffer Kit (cat. no. C10276; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) following the manufacturer’s
instructions. The biotin-alkyne (cat. no. 901995; Sigma‐Aldrich; Merck KGaA) connected palmitic-protein complex
was followed by streptavidin (cat. no. 3419; Cell Signaling Technology, Inc.) pull-down and immunoblot assay for
PD-L1.

Statistical analysis. Statistical analyses were performed by using GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software; Dotmatics).
No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. No data was excluded from the analyses. For data showing
normal distribution, the statistically significant differences between 2 groups of samples were estimated by applying
an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests. One-way ANOVA and Dunnett’s post hoc test were used for comparison
between ≥3 groups. The log-rank test was also applied to assess statistical significance in survival data. Statistical
significance (p-values) was defined as not significant (ns): p > 0.05; *: p < 0.05; **: p < 0.01; ***: p < 0.001. All of
the experiment was independently performed 3 times, each yielding similar results; data from one representative
independent experiment is presented as the mean ± SD.
