involved in resistance of MSI-H/dMMR CRC patients to anti-PD-1 therapy in the clinic.
This conclusion seems potentially odd—if we assume that tumor-expressed PD-L1 acts
by engaging PD-1 on T cells, and if the anti-PD-1 antibody (the specific identity of the
treatment regimen should be stated in methods) was dosed adequately to fully inhibit
PD-1, then why would increase expression of PD-L1 on tumor cells have any bearing
on anti-PD-1 response? Is there any reason to believe that these patients did NOT
receive a dose of anti-PD-1 sufficient for full target coverage?
R: We appreciate this insightful question Although ICB therapy has durable effects
toward a subset of microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) CRCs, accounting for ~15%
of all CRC cases, only 30-50% of these patients can benefit from this therapy. Anti-PD-
1 antibodies work by blocking the interaction between PD-1 on T cells and PD-L1
derived from cancer cells or cells in tumor microenvironments (TME), including
macrophages, MDSCs and fibroblast, thereby enhancing anti-tumor response of CD8+
T cells (J Hematol Oncol. 2021 Jan 7;14(1):10.). Due to intertumoral heterogeneity in
advanced cancer, tumors or other cells may have heterogeneous expression of PD-L1
(J Thorac Dis. 2020 May; 12(5): 1770–1775.). Accordingly, the identification of key
markers in regulating resistance to PD-L1 therapy is necessary to combat an
immunosuppressive TME in CRC. In this study, we discovered that serum GCA/ FXR
signaling could regulate the aberrant expression of SOX14 or DHHC-9, which
persistently induced PD-L1 expression in tumor microenvironments, then affecting the
response to anti-PD-1 therapy. Our findings indicate that combination of targeting the
FXR signaling pathway is a potential strategy for alleviating an immunosuppressive
TME and enhancing the sensitivity to anti-PDL-1 treatment in CRC.
8. Figure 6 (and various associated statements in text): along a similar line, the authors
propose that inhibition of SOX14 or DHHC9 expression in tumors causes an improved
anti-tumor immune response and improved tumor control, presumably via reduced PD-
L1 expression. While this makes sense under untreated conditions, they argue that this
also applies during treatment with anti-PD-1. Similar to the clinical setting, unless PD-
1 blockade is substantially incomplete, it is difficult to understand why alterations in
tumor PD-L1 expression would enhance sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. The data instead
raise the possibility that tumor-intrinsic SOX14/DHHC9 deficiency can act at least
partially in a PD-L1-independent fashion to increase tumor sensitivity to immune
surveillance and anti-PD1 treatment.
R: The reviewer’s comments is thoughtful. As mentioned in response of question 7,
dosage, drug delivery, tumor microenvironment factors, the course of treatment might
affect clinical benefits of anti-PD-1 treatment. To investigate whether the dosage of
anti-PD-1 antibody (100mg/kg) we used could achieve full inhibition, mice
subcutaneous injected of MC38 cells were treated with anti-PD-1 (50mg/kg, 100mg/kg
and 200mg/kg) twice a week starting at day 10 post injection. Our results showed that
anti-PD-1 therapy inhibits MC38 tumorigenesis in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. SS7).
Of note, CRC tumor growth was abolished in mice receiving 200mg/kg of anti-PD-1
antibody treatment (Fig. SS7), suggesting that the dosage used in our in vivo
experiments incompletely in blocking PD-1 on T cells.
Fig. SS7 (A) C57BL/6 (n=6) inoculated with MC38 tumor cells were treated with
indicated dose of anti-PD-1 antibody or IgG 7 days post injection. The tumor volumes
(left) and weights (right) are shown.
9. The MC38 and CT26 models used extensively in this manuscript best represent the
inflamed and potentially immunotherapy-responsive MSI/dMMR subset of CRC.
Have the authors explored whether manipulation of the Fxr pathway impacts immune
responses to 'colder' tumor models that are more representative of sporadic
MSS/pMMR CRCs (which constitute the vast majority of CRC and the bulk of unmet
clinical need). For example, this could include engineered colon organoids (e.g.
Taraborelli et al, Nat Comm, 2023).
R: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. CT26 is often used as an MSS CRC model
due to the lack of mutations in MMR genes MLH1 and MLH2 and is considered to be
a 'cold' tumor model with lower immunogenicity and less responsiveness to
immunotherapy. (BMC Genomics. 2014 Mar 13;15(1):190. Cancer Cell. 2023 Jan
9;41(1):196-209.e5.). In fact, mouse CRC cell lines CT26 and MC-38 exhibited high-
affinity MHC-I-binding neoantigens, indicating that the tumors were susceptible to T-
cell-mediated adaptive immunosurveillance (Nature. 2018 Feb 22;554(7693):538-543.)
Our present study and other separate studies also observed that anti-PD-1 monotherapy
partially limited the outgrowth of CT26 tumors (BMC Cancer. 2021 Nov 13;21(1):1222.
J Exp Clin Cancer Res. 2021 Sep 13;40(1):288.). Moreover, in our study we have also
observed a tumor-promoting role of GCA in both MSS (CT26) and MSI (MC38) CRC
cells. To further validate our results, we used a most common CRC GEMM model by
using ApcMin/+ mouse, which was considered as a model of early MSS CRC (Br J Cancer.
derived from ApcMin/+ mouse into the right flank of C57BL/6, then these mice were
treated with GCA or GW4064 (Fig. SS8). Consistent with our previous observation,
FXR activation profoundly inhibit tumor development, as evidenced by a lower tumor
volume and a better of survival rate of the mice treated with GW4064 than control mice.
Fig. SS8. The tumor volumes of C57BL/6 mice (n=6) inoculated with CRC tumor
sections derived from ApcMin/+ mouse with indicated treatment.

editing recommended.
R: We apologize for the mistakes and have refined the manuscript. In addition, we have
previously sent our revised manuscript for extensively editing.
2. Heatmap scales are generally missing units/labels throughout the figures.
R: We have added the labels of scale bars in our revised manuscript.

Should it actually say, “FXR-mediated tumor suppression…”?
R: Yes, we have reedited this sentence in our revised manuscript.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author): with expertise in bile acids, FXR,
metabolomics
Zhao et al. demonstrated that glycocholic acid (GCA) enhances tumor cell PD-L1
expression, thereby suppressing CD8+ T cell-mediated antitumor responses in the
tumor microenvironment (TME) and promoting colorectal cancer tumor growth. This
effect is mediated through the targeting of the FXR/SOX14/DHHC9 axis. The study
also suggests a testable hypothesis: inhibiting GCA/FXR signaling could augment the
effectiveness of anti-PD-L1 therapy. While this study presents a novel and intriguing
perspective with potential implications for immunotherapy in colorectal cancer (CRC)
patients, several major concerns need to be addressed, and the conclusion lacks robust
evidence.
We are delighted that the reviewer finds our observations interesting. We have
performed point-by-point reply to reviewer as below.
Specific comments are the following:
1. The authors mention the measurement of 33 bile acids (BAs) in serum but fail to
provide a detailed description of the method and BA profiling data. Additionally, the
criteria for defining low and high GCA levels in the recruited population are not clearly
explained. This GCA-based subgrouping method lacks validation in another cohort.
R: We apologize for not clearly describing the detailed method of the measurement of
BAs in our first version of the manuscript. In brief, for the measurement of bile acids
(BAs), 0.1 mL serum sample of CRC patient was mixed with 0.51 ml of ice-cold
MeOH-ACN (1:1, v:v) and sustained under -20 °C for 60 min to precipitate protein.
After 15 min of centrifugation at 14000 rcf under 4℃, the supernatant was aspirated,
and evaporated under vacuum. The residue was dissolved in 100 μl of MeOH and
deionized water (85:15, v:v), and centrifuged at 15000g and 4 °C for 15 min. The
aliquot from the supernatant was injected into the UPLC-MS system for analysis. We
have provided detailed methods in our revised manuscript.
For the definition of low and high GCA levels, we divided the CRC patients into
two groups based on their serum GCA levels. The median concentration of GCA in the
serum of the cohort (Cohort 1 n=80; Cohort 2 n=308) was used as the threshold.
Patients with GCA levels above this mean were classified as GCAhigh, and those below as
GCAlow. Then, Kaplan-Meier survival analyses with log-rank test were used to evaluate
the disease-free and overall survival. In our initial study, we only recruit 80 cancer
patients, we have recruited new 308 CRC patients’ cohort. Our new data also
demonstrated that high serum GCA concentration not only was positively related with
advanced tumor stage but also predict poor overall survival and disease-free survival.
We have updated these results in our manuscript (Fig. SS1A-D, original Figure Fig.
S1C-F).
2. The authors assert that GCA acts as an FXR antagonist based on the Luciferase
reporter assay. However, intra-gastric gavage feeding in animal experiments with GCA
or TβMCA treatment raises concerns about the potential impact of bacterial
transformation of GCA in the gastrointestinal tract. Alternative administration methods,
such as intraperitoneal injection, should be considered.
R: We thank the reviewer’s kind comments. Follow the reviewer’s suggestion, we used
MC38 subcutaneous tumor model to address this issue. In brief, we subcutaneously
injected 1.0×106 MC38 cells diluted in 100 μL of PBS in the right flank of C57BL/6
mice to induce tumor growth. The tumor-bearing mice were i.p. with GCA twice a week
started 7 days post injection. Similarly, our results showed that functional impairment
of FXR by using GCA treatment promoted the tumorigenesis (Fig. SS9 A-B, original
Figure Fig.S3J), suggesting that bacterial transformation of GCA in intestine was not
involved in GCA-induced CRC tumorigenesis.
Fig. SS9. The tumor volumes (left) and tumor mass (right) of C57BL/6 mice (n=6)
inoculated with MC38 tumor cells with or without GCA (i.p., 400mg/kg) treatment.

R: Thanks for your thoughtful comments. In Result 2, we focused on elucidating that
GCA inhibits IFN signaling, which is crucial for anti-tumor immune response.
Therefore, we reedited “To explore the underlying mechanism of GCA-regulated FXR
signaling in promoting CRC,” as follows: “To explore the signaling pathway enriched
in GCA-induced tumorigenesis,”.

Clarification is needed.

experiments for this section and reedited the sentence “Inhibition of GCA/FXR-induced
SOX14 and DHHC9 expression sensitizes CRC to anti-PD-L1 therapy.” as follows:
“Inhibition of GCA/FXR-induced SOX14 and DHHC9 expression sensitizes CRC to

7. Representative tumor graphs for all in vivo animal experiments should be provided
by the authors.
R: Thanks for your suggestion. While providing representative tumor graphs for all in
vivo animal experiments can enhance credibility of our results, large-scale experiments
involving a significant number of animals, resulting in an extensive amount of image
data. Due to the limitation of the space of our manuscripts, presenting all these images

metronidazole? enhancing GCA-induced resistant tumors to ICB therapy without

9. Detailed recruitment criteria information for the two cohorts, including healthy
subjects, should be provided.?
R: Thank you for your thorough review of our manuscript. According to this comment,
we have described the detailed recruitment criteria information for all CRC patients’
cohorts and healthy subjects in our revised manuscript as following: One cohort of 80
paired CRC tissues (Cohort 1), adjacent normal mucosa tissues and serum collected
between January 2018 and September 2018 from patients with CRC who were
diagnosed at Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center (FUSCC) were recruited.
Another cohort of 308 patients (Cohort 2) with CRC between January 2008 and
September 2009, who were diagnosed at Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center to
validate our results that high serum GCA concentration not only was positively related
with advanced tumor stage but also predict poor overall survival and disease-free
survival. The clinicopathological characteristics of all patients in these 2 cohorts were

Human serum specimens were collected prior to tumor resection, while normal mucosa

R: Thank you! Indeed, the tumor-bearing mice were treated with GCA via intragastric
gavage. We have reedited the words "GCA diet" in line 27 as follows:” GCA treatment”.
11. The rationale behind the test doses for BA-related agents in vivo and in vitro should
be illustrated, and the method needs supplementation
R: The dosage for BA-related agents, including GW4064 and T-βMCA used in our in
vitro experiments was primarily based on references from previous studies (Cell. 2019
Feb 21; 176(5): 1098–1112.e18.). We have provided this information in the method
section of our revised manuscript. For the dosage of GCA used in vivo, we administered
GCA at 0 mg/kg to 800 mg/kg p.o., twice a week, beginning at day that MC38 tumors
reached ~100mm3 post subcutaneous injection of C57/BL6 mice. Tumorigenesis was
robustly promoted in mice treated with 400 mg/kg or 800 mg/kg of GCA (Fig. SS10 A,
original Figure Fig.S3B). However, a high dose of GCA (800 mg/kg) treatment
increased tumor burden with evident side effects as measured by weight loss during the
cause (Fig. SS10 A-B, original Figure Fig.S3B). Therefore, we used 400 mg/kg of GCA
to perform our in vivo experiments. In addition, we cultured MC38 cells with 0-200µM
of GCA and observed that GCA suppressed FXR activity in a dose dependent manner
(Fig. SS10 C, original Figure Fig.S2D). Of note, 100µM of GCA robustly decreased
the activation of FXR without affecting the proliferation of MC38 cells (Fig. SS10 C
and D, original Figure Fig.S2D), suggesting that this dosage of GCA is optimal for in
vitro experiments. We have provided these results in our revised manuscript.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author): with expertise in PD-L1 regulation, cancer
immunology
Zhao et al. demonstrated that GCA accumulates in the serum of patients with CRC. This
accumulation leads to a reduced activity of the bile acid receptor FXR, resulting in a
poor antitumor CD8+ T cell response. Mechanistically, GCA upregulates tumor PD-L1
expression through the FXR-SOX14-DHHC9 axis-mediated palmitoylation of PD-L1.
While the study includes substantial experiments, it lacks novelty in terms of the role
of GCA and its receptor in CRC and the palmitoylation of PD-L1 by DHHC9, as these
have been reported in previous studies.
We appreciate the reviewer’s insight comments. We have addressed the specific
question raised by the reviewer.
Major concerns:
1. The pre-diagnostic plasma GCA levels and colon cancer risk has already been
reported (PMID: 31435679), as well as the mechanism regarding the role of DHHC9
on the expression of PD-L1 (PMID: 30514902). In addition, the bile acid receptor FXR
agonist GW4064 has already been reported to enhance anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy in
colorectal cancer (PMID: 37261088). Thus, the key points of this study are already
known with less novelty.
A: We truly appreciate the reviewer's insightful comments on our observation. In this
study, we have identified GCA is a risk factor for colorectal cancer, and mechanistically
dissected of GCA-induced tumorigenesis by promoting SOX14/DHHC9-mediated
palmitoylation and stabilization of PD-L1. Based on these results, we are the first to
propose and prove that the serum GCA is not only a pre-diagnostic marker, but also a
driver of CRC. Additionally, we observed that GCA increased SOX14 expression via
inhibiting FXR activity, and resulted in a transcriptional regulation of DHHC9, which
filled the missing linkage on how FXR regulates immune suppressive environments
through stabilizing PD-L1. We considered this to be one of the innovative aspects of
our findings. As pointed out by the reviewer, it has been reported that FXR agonist
GW4064 sensitized anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy in CRC, which reduces the originality
of our manuscript (Oncoimmunology. 2023 May 25;12(1):2217024.). While totally
agreeing with this reviewer, we would like to draw his or her attention to our result that
the combined therapy of GW4064 and anti-PD-1 antibody sufficiently attenuated
tumorigenesis of anti-PD-1 resistant CRC or CRC in mice with high concentration of
GCA, which further strengthened this point by broadening the range of indications for
this combined therapy.
2.The cluster identification by scRNA-seq in Figure 2 is not reasonable. The resolution
seems very low and rough because no other myeloid clusters, such as dendritic cells,
MDSCs, and neutrophils, or T-cell subsets (cytotoxic or exhausted), or tumor cells were
found in the scRNA-seq. The cell population in scRNA-seq seems exactly the same as
that found by flow cytometry. Especially, the macrophage population is the largest
among tumor-infiltrating immune cells and is heterogeneous. What markers were used
to identify the macrophages? No gene expression data were shown for each cluster.
R: We appreciate the reviewer’s careful reading of our manuscript and apologize for
not clearly describing the method that we defined clusters in our first version of the
manuscript and any confusion it might have caused. We have provided detailed methods
for scRNA-seq data preprocessing in our revised manuscript (Supplementary materials
and methods/ Single-cell RNA-seq data preprocessing). In brief, highly variable genes
were selected by using Seurat’s FindVariableGenes function (mean.function =
FastExpMean, dispersion.function = FastLogVMR) for Principal Component Analysis
(PCA). We identified cell clones by performing graph-based clustering (FindNeighbors
function in Seurat) and visualized the cells using a 2-dimensional t-distributed
stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE, RunTSNE function in Seurat). FindAllMarkers
function was performed to select positive or unique markers for cell clones compared
with other clones. Then, we used R package SingleR, with the reference transcriptomic
datasets ‘Human Primary Cell Atlas’ to identify five major clusters of immune cells,
CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, macrophages, B cells, neutrophils and NK cells (BMC
Genomics. 2013 Sep 20; 14:632.). It seems that neutrophils were barely detectible based
on our scRNA-sequencing. Considering that deletion of macrophages had little effect
on GCA-mediated tumorigenesis, we did not re-cluster the identified macrophages to
further analysis. In addition, we used a panel of 21 detectable genes in our system
(Fig.SS11, original Figure Fig.S6A), which was reported as markers for inferring
immune cell populations in time-of-flight (CyTOF) analysis (Fig4A, Cancer Discovery.
enriched in typical clusters of immune cells as shown below, including CD3ε and CD4α
for CD4+ T cells, CD3ε and CD8α for CD8+ T cells, ITGAM (CD11b) and ADGRE1
(F4/80) for macrophages, CD19 and CD68 for B cells as well as NKG7 and XCL1 for
NKs, suggesting the methods we used were suitable for characterizing the cell of origin
of each of the single cells. Therefore, we analyzed these immune cell populations in
MC38 tumors treated with GCA to validate our results that FXR promoted the tumor-
infiltrating CD8+ T cells observed in MC38 tumors treated with FXR agonist GW4064
based on scRNA-sequencing.
Fig. SS11 Tumors from C57BL/6 mice treated with GW4064 on day 16 were subjected
to single-cell RNA sequencing analysis (n=3), markers of immune subtypes, including
CD3ε and CD4α for CD4+ T cells, CD3ε and CD8α for CD8+ T cells, CD68 and C1QA
for macrophages, CD19 and CD68 for B cells as well as NKG7 and XCL1 for NKs,
markers of immune activation and inflammatory markers were selected. Heatmap for
the average expression level of indicated immune markers were shown (Z-score
normalized).

clinical relevance between GCA and patient outcome. Are SOX14, GCA, and DHHC9
expression associated with patient survival in other studies? They should provide more

results in newly recruited CRC cohort (Cohort 2 n=308). We had divided CRC patients
into two groups by mean concentration of GCA in serum and found that high serum
GCA concentration was not only positively related with advanced tumor stage but also
predict poor overall survival and disease-free survival. Moreover, IHC staining assay
and non-parametric spearman correlation analyses revealed that the serum

or DHHC9, which further validate our results that high serum GCA concentration of
CRC patients is linked to poorly prognosis (Fig. SS12, original Figure Fig.S10A-C).
We have supplemented these results in our revised manuscript.

5. In figures 4 and 6, all the in vivo mouse models are performed by subcutaneous
injection. The tumor microenvironment differs significantly in different organs, so
orthotopic models should be performed to validate the authors' conclusions.
R: As per your kind suggestion, we generated an orthotopic mice model of CRC by
injecting MC38 cells with Matrigel into colon mucosa. In brief, 0.5×106 SOX14-KD
(knockdown) and control MC38 cells mixed with 10 μL of Matrigel were injected into

Figures 4 was started 10 days post injection. Tumor weights were measured at endpoint.
We found that SOX14-knockdown profoundly inhibited GCA-induced tumorigenesis
(Fig. SS15A, original Figure Fig.S9G). In addition, tumors with SOX14-knockdown
showed an enhanced population of CD8+ and IFNγ+ CD8+ T cells, accompanied with

Furthermore, we used this autochthonous mouse CRC tumor model to evaluate whether

and anti-PD-1 antibody significantly inhibited the tumorigenesis of anti-PD-1-resistant
MC38 cells (Fig. SS15C, original Figure Fig.S11G). Of note, tumors receiving
combined therapy showed an increased population of infiltrating CD8+ IFNγ+ T effector
cell and a decreased percentage of exhausted T cells compared to tumors with
monotherapies (Fig. SS15D, original Figure Fig.S11H), which further validate our
conclusion that combined FXR agonist with anti-PD-1 therapy enhanced the efficacy
of anti-PD-1 in CRC.

MC38R (C-D) cells were endoscopy-guided injected into C57BL/6J mice (n=6). (A, C)
Tumor volumes of the indicated mice were shown. (B, D) The percentages of CD8+ T
cells from CD45+ cells (left), and frequencies of exhausted CD8+ T cells (TIM3+,

Minor concerns:
6. What is the reason for the difference in GCA levels between healthy individuals and
patients with CRC?
R: We are truly thankful to this reviewer for his or her interesting thoughts on
glycocholic acid (GCA) GCA. GCA, a primary bile acid, is formed by cholic acid (CA)
amidated with glycine in liver, and then released into the intestine (Nat Rev
Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2024 Apr 4.). It is natural that the levels of GCA are tightly
regulated by liver function. CRC can affect liver function either directly (through
metastasis) or indirectly (through systemic inflammation or metabolic changes),
potentially leading to altered GCA levels. In addition, bile acids, including GCA, are
absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and transported via the portal blood to the liver
(Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2022 Jul;19(7):432-450.). CRC can affect the
gastrointestinal tract's ability to absorb and excrete various metabolites, which may lead
to differences in GCA levels between healthy individuals and CRC patients
(Metabolites. 2021 Mar 10;11(3):159.). Of note, the gut microbiota plays a crucial role
in bile acid metabolism (Nat Rev Microbiol. 2023 Apr;21(4):236-247.). Long-term
antibiotic treatment significantly increased glycocholic acid (Front Microbiol. 2022 Jun
29:13:832915.). It is known that composition of the gut microbiota is altered in faecal
samples and in tumor-associated communities of CRC patients compared to healthy
people, which may influence GCA levels (Front Physiol. 2022 May 4:13:854545.).
Collectively, the difference in serum GCA levels between healthy individuals and
patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) can be attributed to several factors, such as liver
function, intestinal absorption and excretion as well as microbiota alterations.
7.Macrophage depleted efficiency in Figure 2e should be detected.
R: Following your kind suggestion, Fasc analysis was used to determine the depleted
efficiency of macrophages in MC38 tumors. Our results showed that the percentage of
macrophages was significantly decreased in tumors derived from mice treated with
clodronates compared to controls (Fig. SS16, original Figure Fig.S6B), suggesting that

This study shows that glycocholic acid (GCA) is associated with human colon cancer
and that GCA promoted colon tumorigenesis in cultured colon cancer cell lines in
immunocompetent xenograph mouse models through GCA inhibition of FXR signaling
that altered the expression of target genes involved in immunomodulation of tumor
growth by anti-PD-L1 and PD-1 drugs (such as nivolumab, pembrolizumab,
atezolizumab, avelumab, aurvalumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab and retifanlimab).
While FXR has been shown to be involved in repression of colon and liver cancer in a
number of earlier studies, this is a novel mechanism if it can be substantiated by
experimentation. The authors propose that this effect is a result of GCA antagonism of
FXR. However, GCA has never been shown to be an FXR antagonist while TCA
(taurine conjugate of CA), found in mice, is a potent FXR agonist. And others showed

clear whether is the result of colon cancer or in increased by other means such as

mechanism of the anti-tumor effect is dependent on FXR expression in the tumor cells
where the authors suggest that when FXR signaling is inhibited by GCA, it leads to PD-
L1 palmitoylation via DHHC9 and PD-L1 stabilization. While the data are interesting
and the effect of FXR agonist clear and convincing, the data on GCA as an FXR
antagonist is not convincing and not in agreement with earlier studies.

5. Mice are not a good model to study the effects of GCA since mice make trace
amounts of GCA; they mostly make the taurine conjugate TCA. But they are a good
model to study the therapeutic effects of GCA. This should be discussed.
R: We appreciate the reviewer’s comments and the insightful thoughts provided. It is
indeed true that humans and mice exhibit substantially different bile acid pool
compositions. In humans, bile acids in the liver are conjugated (N-acyl-amidated)
with glycine (G) or taurine (T) in a ratio of approximately 3 to 1. In contrast, mice
predominantly use taurine for conjugation, with over 95% of their bile acids being
taurine conjugated. Humans produce a diverse mix of bile acids, including a substantial
amount of glycochenodeoxycholic acid (GCA). Conversely, mice predominantly
synthesize taurocholic acid (TCA), and only trace amounts of GCA are found in their
system. This difference in endogenous bile acid composition presents a challenge when
studying the physiological effects of GCA in mice, as their natural bile acid
environment differs significantly from that of humans. Due to the low endogenous
levels of GCA in mice, which are highly amenable to study the mechanisms,
function or therapeutic effects of GCA by exogenously administered GCA. In our studies,
we observed that GCA inhibited the transcriptional function of the Farnesoid X Receptor
(FXR) in both human and colorectal cancer (CRC) cells. Importantly, GCA was found
to promote tumor growth in mice and is identified as a high-risk factor for CRC
tumorigenesis, suggesting a tumor-promoting function in CRC. These results highlight
the relevance of using mouse models to study the therapeutic effects of GCA, despite
the differences in bile acid composition between species.
We have addressed this point in detail in our revised manuscript, discussing both the
limitations and the strengths of using mice as a model for GCA research in our revised
manuscripts.

transport, digestion and absorption of nutrients, particularly lipids and lipid-soluble
vitamins. Up to 95 % of bile acids are actively re-absorbed in the terminal ileum and
transported back to the liver and enter the systemic circulation. it has been suggested
that blood levels of bile acids could be more useful to investigate associations with
cancer risk than fecal bile acids, and small case-control studies have found increased
serum bile acids levels in patients with colon cancer.10-12 In fact, we have already
evaluated the concentrations of bile acid (BA) concentrations in tumor tissue from small
samples, the concentrations were very low, thus we did not show these data and chose
the blood levels of bile acids for further study.

The most important pathway of BA signaling for regulating the development of
intestinal cancer is through the nuclear receptor FXR, which suppresses colorectal
tumorigenesis with a tumor cell intrinsic mechanism.21,26,27 In mouse models, loss of
FXR expression was associated with increased size and number of CRC tumors via
promoting Wnt signaling or increasing the proliferation of Lgr5+ intestinal stem
cells.21,27 (PMID: 18981289) Conversely, the FXR agonist GW4064 counteracted

Given the difference in the growth of tumor cells between in culture and in vivo
observed in our previous studies, we found that inactivation of FXR significantly
promoted CRC tumorigeneses in a cell extrinsic mechanism by suppressing the
infiltration and antitumor function of CD8+ T cells. IFNg secreted by CD8+ T cells
suppressed tumor cells through inhibiting proliferation and inducing apoptosis,
differentiation, migration, and cell-surface antigen expression, which give at least
partially explanation on the suppressive function of FXR in regulating cell proliferation
in vivo.

(LCA) exacerbate CRC through cytotoxicity and genotoxicity, increasing oxidative
stress and DNA damage in colonic epithelial cells (Nat Rev Microbiol. 2023
Apr;21(4):236-247.). Gut microbiota plays a critical role by converting primary to
secondary BAs, with dysbiosis linked to higher CRC risk (Nature. 2020
Jun;582(7813):566-570. Gut Microbes. 2022 Jan-Dec;14(1):2132903.). For example,
BSH-expressing Bacteroides is often found in CRC patients with overweight and
trigger large amounts of unconjugated bile acids in the colon, leading to the progression
of CRC (PMID: 36765047). GCA treatment significantly promoted tumor growth in
our study. The role of gut microbiota in GCA-induced tumorigenesis is indeed a critical
field of interest for future research. Nevertheless, based on our findings, we exerted the
tumor-inhibitory effects of FXR in vivo to the dependency of host conditions. In our
study, it was found that the inactivation of FXR significantly suppressed the infiltration
and antitumor function of CD8+ T cells by increasing the expression of PD-L1 in tumor
cells. It has been reported that primary BAs and FXR ligands negatively regulate the
IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α release from LPS-primed macrophages.28 Although increased
infiltration of F4/80+ macrophages was also observed in tumors with GCA treatment,
the faster growth of GCA-treated tumors was abolished only in CD8+ T cells-depleted,
but not in macrophages-depleted, mice. This indicated that impeding the antitumor
function of CD8+ T cells in the TME was essential for GCA-mediated tumor outgrowth.”

REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a highly prevalent tumor type that is generally refractory to immunotherapy. Thus, elucidating
mechanisms of CRC resistance to immunotherapy is of high importance. In this study, Zhao et al make use of a comprehensive
range of clinical data, in vivo models, and in vitro cell biology assays to identify bile acids as potential regulators of CRC sensitivity
to T cell attack. Mechanistically, this is proposed to occur through the bile acid nuclear receptor Fxr, which regulates expression
of SOX14 and the palmitoyltransferase DHHC9 to control palmitoylation and stability of the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1.
Overall, the authors responded satisfactorily to my suggestions from the initial review, with several new experiments and analyses
provided to support their claims. However, I have some remaining suggestions that should be addressed prior to publication:
A: We appreciate the reviewer’s acknowledgment of our additional experiments and analyses, and we are pleased that they find
our revisions satisfactory overall. We carefully reviewed the remaining suggestions and have addressed each point.

2. Association of serum GCA concentrations with patient survival:
In my previous comments, I made the following suggestion: It would be interesting/informative to compare BA concentrations in
patients with liver vs non-liver metastases and include liver metastasis specifically as a covariate in survival analysis (as distinct
from other metastatic sites)
The authors have evaluated a larger (n=308) CRC cohort in an effort to address this question but concluded that the number of
patients with liver metastasis (35 with liver only) is too small to enable robust conclusions. I agree that the small number of liver
mets in this cohort is statistically limiting and makes it difficult to draw conclusions about the liver met+ patient segment. However,
the authors could additionally evaluate the relationship between PFS/OS and serum BA in patients without metastasis—if a PFS/OS
association is observed in patients with earlier stage disease, it would increase confidence that the clinical observations are
independent of liver metastasis.
A: We thank the reviewer for the insightful follow-up suggestion. In response, we have performed additional survival analyses
focusing on colorectal cancer (CRC) patients with documented disease-free survival (DFS) and no evidence of liver metastases (n
= 247) to assess the association between serum GCA concentrations and clinical outcomes. Kaplan–Meier analyses demonstrated
that higher serum GCA concentrations remained significantly associated with both shorter disease-free survival (DFS) and overall
survival (OS) in this subgroup. These results reinforce our original observation that elevated serum GCA levels are linked to poor
clinical outcomes in CRC and suggest that this association is independent of the presence of liver metastases (Fig.SS1, original
Fig.S1G-H).

the cut-off value.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
I appreciate the revisions to the manuscript resubmitted by the authors. With new experiments they have addressed many of
my concerns. Nevertheless, I still have the following concerns:
A: We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the revisions and additional experiments we have performed. Below, we address the
remaining concerns point by point.
1. This manuscript demonstrates limited novelty, particularly regarding the clinical role of GW4064 in immunotherapy and the
regulatory mechanisms of PD-L1.
A: We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the novelty of our findings. While it has been previously reported that FXR
agonist GW4064 enhances anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy efficacy in CRC (Lu et al., Oncoimmunology, 2023), our study offers
additional mechanistic and translational insights that we believe add novel value to the field.
Bile acids (BAs) play a dual role in regulating tumorigenesis, and different bile acid species exert distinct effects. Recent studies
have provided emerging evidence that several BAs, including deoxycholic acid (DCA) and lithocholic acid (LCA), are critical for
shaping tumor microenvironment to induce tumor evasion (Cong et al., Immunity, 2024; Varanasi et al., Science, 2025). Therefore,
distinguishing among BA species and elucidating their mechanism of regulating tumor-TME crosstalk is essential.
In our study, we identify GCA not only as a pre-diagnostic serum biomarker but also as a functional driver of colorectal
tumorigenesis, acting through the SOX14/DHHC9/PD-L1 axis. We further demonstrate that GCA promotes PD-L1 stability via
FXR inhibition and downstream transcriptional activation of SOX14 and DHHC9, providing a previously unrecognized
mechanistic link between FXR signaling and PD-L1 palmitoylation.
Moreover, we show that combined treatment with GW4064 and anti-PD-1 antibody effectively suppresses tumor growth even in
anti-PD-1–resistant CRC models and in mice with elevated GCA levels. These findings not only support and extend prior
observations but also broaden the therapeutic applicability of FXR agonist-based immunotherapy, particularly in GCA-enriched
CRC subsets. We believe this mechanistic and translational depth offers meaningful innovation beyond previously published work.

In response, we have now included representative tumor images from the indicated experimental groups in the revised Figure S1-

efficacy. These images were integrated in the in Supplementary Figure 13 (Fig.S13) of the revised manuscript.

manuscript. Scale bars have been added to “Merge” panel of Fig. 5B. Molecular weight markers have been labeled on each blot to
indicate protein size.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
THe response to the reviewers are incomplete.
Q1&2. There is no evidence that GCA as an FXR antagonist as established in many earlier studies. This critical issue is not
addressed. GCA and other derived bile acids in serum and tumor tissues should be measured after GCA administration in vivo.
What are the median concentrations of GCA in cohort 1 and cohort 2? Is it above 100 µM or below 100 µM? As shown in figure
SS10C, there was no dose effect on FXR inhibition when GCA concentration was 100 µM or more.
A: We sincerely thank the reviewer for these insightful and detailed comments and acknowledge the reviewer’s important point
regarding the mechanistic classification of GCA.
1. On GCA as an FXR antagonist:
We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern that the classification of GCA as an FXR antagonist remains a matter of ongoing
investigation. While previous reports have demonstrated that GCA can inhibit FXR activity in human cancer cells (Dai et al.,
Journal of Hematology & Oncology, 2011), there is limited direct evidence establishing this function at physiological
concentrations in vivo. Accordingly, we do not assert that GCA acts as a classical pharmacological antagonist. Instead, our data
suggests that GCA exposure is associated with reduced FXR activity in CRC, as indicated by downregulation of canonical FXR
target genes (e.g., Shp, Fgf15) and concomitant increases in PD-L1 expression.
2. On bile acid concentrations in vivo (serum and tumor):
Regarding the in vivo GCA treatment, we agree that endogenous and systemic bile acid levels are critical to interpreting the data.
As suggested, we measured the concentrations of GCA and other bile acids, specifically TDCA, TCA, TCDCA, GCDCA, and
GDCA, which are significantly elevated in the serum of CRC patients compared to healthy individuals (Fig.1A), following GCA
administration (400 mg/kg) in a subcutaneous MC38 tumor model. Consistent with previous reports, serum GCA levels were barely
detectable in healthy mice or in tumor-bearing mice without GCA treatment. In contrast, several serum levels of other bile acids
were elevated in MC38 tumor-bearing mice relative to healthy controls. Of note, a detectable accumulation of serum GCA
approximately 150 nM was observed in serum of mice receiving GCA treatment. In tumor tissues, GCA levels remained low in
mice untreated, while the concentration was measurable, with a concentration of approximately 82 nmol/g in GCA-treated tumors
(Fig.SS2A, B, original Fig.S3C, D).
As shown in Figure SS10C of our previous response, we treated cultured cells with 1 mL of complete DMEM containing 100 nM
(100 nmol/L) GCA. We have carefully reviewed our data and apologize for the earlier labeling error, where "100 μM" (equivalent
to 100 nmol/mL) was mistakenly used instead of the correct "100 nM" (100 nmol/L), due to a unit conversion issue. At and above
100 nM GCA-treatment in vitro, we observed effective FXR inhibition, evidenced by reduced FXRE-luciferase reporter activity
in treated cells compared to untreated controls (Fig.S2B).
Importantly, the median GCA concentration in mouse serum after GCA treatment (157.48 nM) falls within the range that has been
shown to inhibit FXR signaling under experimental conditions (100-200nM). Furthermore, the median serum GCA concentrations
in our human cohorts were approximately 96.4 nM in Cohort 1 and 96.7 nM in Cohort 2. These values are comparable to or slightly
lower than those observed in GCA-treated mice and in vitro cultures, supporting the physiological relevance of our experimental
models.
Fig. SS2. (A, B) The serum (A) or tumoral (B) concentration of indicated BAs in healthy mice or mice inoculated with MC38 cells
following indicated GCA treatment (400mg/kg, n=6).
3. Although there is sufficient data showing that FXR signaling was suppressed in mice treated with 400 mg/kg GCA, it is unknown
whether the serum levels of GCA obtained under this treatment is within the range of that found in humans, which is very important
to determine the translational value of this study.
A: We appreciate the reviewer’s important point regarding the translational relevance of the GCA dosing used in our mouse model.
As outlined above, we have now quantified serum GCA concentrations in mice treated with 400 mg/kg GCA. The median GCA
level was approximately 157.48 nM, which is slightly higher than the median serum GCA concentrations (~100nM) observed in
CRC patients.
Thus, the serum GCA levels achieved in our mouse model are not only comparable to those in human CRC patients but also fall
within the same order of magnitude. This concordance supports the translational relevance of our dosing regimen. Importantly, the
observed suppression of FXR signaling and associated immunological changes in GCA-treated mice occurred at physiologically
relevant concentrations, further underscoring the clinical significance of our findings.
8. To determine if Fxr-null mice are more resistant than WT mice to anti-PD-L1 therapy, four groups of mice are needed, i.e. WT
vehicle, WT anti-PD-L1, Fxr null vehicle, Fxr null anti-PD-L1. In addition to the comparisons between WT and Fxr null mice,
like the authors had done in Figure SS19, the comparisons between vehicle and anti-PD-L1 groups are needed to evaluate the effect of
anti-PD-L1 treatment. In fact, if you compare the data in Figure SS18 and Figure SS19, there was almost no improvement in tumor
number and tumor area between FXR WT mock group and FXR WT anti-PD-L1 group, suggesting that WT mice were almost
completely resistant to anti-PD-L1 therapy.
A: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive comment. We fully agree that evaluating the effect of anti-PD-L1
therapy requires the inclusion of all four groups: Fxrwt + IgG, Fxrwt + anti-PD-L1, Fxr-/- + IgG, and Fxr-/- + anti-PD-L1, to allow
direct comparisons both within and between genotypes.
In our study, we utilized Fxr-knockout (Fxr-/-) and their littermate wild-type (Fxrwt) controls in the AOM/DSS-induced CRC model
to assess the response to anti-PD-L1 treatment. While the comparisons of tumor number and tumor area in mice between Fxrwt
mock group of Figure SS18 and Fxrwt anti-PD-1α group of Figure SS19 did not appear significantly different in our previous
responses, it is important to note that these data were derived from independent experiments, and minor discrepancies could be due
to biological variability between mouse batches or age ranges.
In our repeated experiments using four groups, we observed that anti-PD-L1 treatment at dosage of 10mg/kg significantly reduced
tumor burden in Fxrwt mice, indicating a robust response to therapy in the WT background. More importantly, anti-PD-L1 therapy
in Fxr-/- mice resulted in marked acceleration in both tumor number and tumor area, as well as shorter colon length, compared to
Fxrwt mice receiving the same treatment (Fig.SS3, original Fig.S7J). This reduction of therapeutic efficacy in Fxr-deficient mice
underscores our central conclusion: Fxr-deficiency inhibits the response of the tumor microenvironment to PD-1/PD-L1 immune
checkpoint blockade.
Fig.SS3. Fxr-knockout mice (Fxr-/-) and their litter mates (Fxrwt) were injected with anti-PD-L1 antibody (10mg/kg) or IgG (i.g.)
during AOM/DSS treatment (n=6 per group). Colon length (left), tumor numbers (middle) and tumor areas (right) of colons were
shown.
